The accounts of Government Companies and Government controlled other Companies, set up under 
the provisions of the Companies Act, are audited by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India 
(CAG) under the provisions of Section 143 of the Companies Act, 2013. The accounts certified by 
the Statutory Auditors (Chartered Accountants) appointed by the CAG under the Companies Act 
are subject to supplementary audit by officers of the CAG and the CAG gives his comments or 
supplements the reports of the Statutory Auditors under section 143(6) of the Companies Act, 2013.  
In addition, these Companies are also subject to test audit by CAG under the provisions of Section 
143(7) of the Companies Act, 2013. 
The statutes governing some Corporations and Authorities require their accounts to be audited by 
CAG. In respect of six such Corporations viz., Airports Authority of India, National Highways 
Authority of India, Inland Waterways Authority of India, Food Corporation of India, Damodar 
Valley Corporation and National Cooperative Development Corporation, the relevant statutes 
designate CAG as their sole auditor. In respect of one Corporation viz., Centra l Warehousing 
Corporation, auditor is appointed by the Government, on the advice of the CAG, for audit of the 
accounts of the Central Warehousing Corporation. CAG has the right to conduct the audit as he 
may consider necessary. 
Reports in relation to the accounts of a Government Company or Corporation are submitted to the 
Government by CAG for laying before the Parliament under the provisions of Section 19-A of the 
Comptroller and Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. 
This General Purpose Financial Reports of Central Public Sector Enterprises for the year ended 31 
March, 2024 contains eight chapters namely, Summary of Financial Performance of Central Public 
Sector Enterprises, Oversight Role of CAG, Corporate Governance, Exp enditure in Research and 
Development by CPSEs, Corporate Social Responsibility, Analysis of Memoranda of 
Understanding between Administrative Ministries and Navratna CPSEs, Disinvestment in CPSEs 
and Review of Sustainability Status. In respect of CPSEs where any particular year’s accounts were 
not received before 31 December, 2024, the figures from the accounts last audited have been 
adopted. In respect of some CPSEs of Chapter-I, figures for the previous year might not agree with 
the corresponding figur es shown in the Audit Report No.23 of 2025 owing to replacement of 
provisional figures by audited/revised figures. 
All references to ‘Companies/Corporations or CPSEs’ in this Report may be construed to refer to 
‘Central Government Companies/Corporations’ unless the context suggests otherwise. 
The audit has been conducted in conformity with the Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller 
and Auditor General of India. 
Audit wishes to acknowledge the cooperation received from the Managements of CPSEs and their 
respective Administrative Ministries/Departments at each stage of audit process.

Introduction 
There were 757 Central Government Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) under the audit jurisdiction 
of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India as on 31 March, 2024. These included 521 
Government companies, 229 Government controlled other companies and seven Statutory 
Corporations. This Report presents financial performance of 684 CPSEs which includes 479 
Government companies and Corporations (including seven Statutory Corporations) and 205 
Government controlled other companies. 73  CPSEs (including 24 Government controlled other  
companies), whose accounts were in arrears for three years or more or were under liquidation or 
first accounts were not due/received, are not covered in this Report. 
(Para 1.1.3) 
Investment of Central Government  
The accounts of 479 Government companies a nd Corporations indicated that the Central 
Government had an equity holding of ₹11,93,439 crore in share capital as on 31 March, 2024.  The 
long term loans given by Central Government to such CPSEs outstanding as on 31 March 2024 
amounted to ₹2,87,678 crore. Compared to the previous year, holding of the Central Government 
in equity of such CPSEs registered a net increase of ₹2,68,767 crore and long term loans outstanding 
increased by ₹1,63,332 crore during 2023-24.           
(Para 1.2, 1.2.1 and 1.2.2.1) 
Market Capitalisation 
The total market value of shares of 66 listed Government companies (including nine subsidiary 
companies and excluding three newly listed CPSEs during the year), the shares of which were 
traded during 2023 -24, stood at ₹37,92,736 crore as on 31 March, 2024. Market value of shares 
held by the Central Government in these 66 listed Government companies (including nine 
subsidiary companies) stood at ₹23,51,459 crore as on 31 March, 2024.      
 (Para 1.2.4) 
 
Returns from Government companies and Corporations 
 282 Government companies and Corporations earned profit of ₹3,58,385 crore during 2023-24 of 
which, 70.46 per cent  (₹2,52,535 crore) was contributed by 79 CPSEs in three sectors viz., 
Petroleum, Power and Coal & Lignite. Return on Equity (ROE) of these 282 CPSEs was 16.28 per 
cent in 2023-24 as compared to 13.75 per cent of 259 CPSEs in 2022-23.  
                                                                                                                  (Para 1.3.1) 
134 Government companies and Corporations declared a dividend of ₹1,38,138 crore for the year 
2023-24. Out of this, the dividend received/receivable by Central Government amounted to ₹65,071

Introduction 
There were 757 Central Government Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) under the audit jurisdiction 
of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India as on 31 March, 2024. These included 521 
Government companies, 229 Government controlled other companies and seven Statutory 
Corporations. This Report presents financial performance of 684 CPSEs which includes 479 
Government companies and Corporations (including seven Statutory Corporations) and 205 
Government controlled other companies. 73  CPSEs (including 24 Government controlled other  
companies), whose accounts were in arrears for three years or more or were under liquidation or 
first accounts were not due/received, are not covered in this Report. 
(Para 1.1.3) 
Investment of Central Government  
The accounts of 479 Government companies a nd Corporations indicated that the Central 
Government had an equity holding of ₹11,93,439 crore in share capital as on 31 March, 2024.  The 
long term loans given by Central Government to such CPSEs outstanding as on 31 March 2024 
amounted to ₹2,87,678 crore. Compared to the previous year, holding of the Central Government 
in equity of such CPSEs registered a net increase of ₹2,68,767 crore and long term loans outstanding 
increased by ₹1,63,332 crore during 2023-24.           
(Para 1.2, 1.2.1 and 1.2.2.1) 
Market Capitalisation 
The total market value of shares of 66 listed Government companies (including nine subsidiary 
companies and excluding three newly listed CPSEs during the year), the shares of which were 
traded during 2023 -24, stood at ₹37,92,736 crore as on 31 March, 2024. Market value of shares 
held by the Central Government in these 66 listed Government companies (including nine 
subsidiary companies) stood at ₹23,51,459 crore as on 31 March, 2024.      
 (Para 1.2.4) 
 
Returns from Government companies and Corporations 
 282 Government companies and Corporations earned profit of ₹3,58,385 crore during 2023-24 of 
which, 70.46 per cent  (₹2,52,535 crore) was contributed by 79 CPSEs in three sectors viz., 
Petroleum, Power and Coal & Lignite. Return on Equity (ROE) of these 282 CPSEs was 16.28 per 
cent in 2023-24 as compared to 13.75 per cent of 259 CPSEs in 2022-23.  
                                                                                                                  (Para 1.3.1) 
134 Government companies and Corporations declared a dividend of ₹1,38,138 crore for the year 
2023-24. Out of this, the dividend received/receivable by Central Government amounted to ₹65,071

crore which represented 5.45 per cent return on the total investment by the Central Government 
(₹11,93,439 crore) in equity capital of all the 479 Government companies and Corporations. 
Eleven Government companies under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas contributed

Losses/Accumulated Losses   
182 Government companies incurred losses amounting to ₹34,908 crore during the year 2023 -24. 
There were 214 Government companies with accumulated losses of ₹2,47,181 crore as on 31 
March, 2024. Of these, the net worth of 91  companies had been completely eroded by their 
accumulated losses. As a result, the aggregate net worth of these companies had become negative 
to the extent of ₹58,175 crore as on 31 March 2024. Twen ty-One out of these 91  CPSEs earned 
profit of ₹961 crore during the year 2023-24. 
(Para 1.3.2 and 1.3.3.1) 
Sales and Marketing 
Total sales by 479 Government companies and Corporations was ₹36,44,513 crore. Out of these 
CPSEs, 117 CPSEs sold goods/rendered services worth ₹3,94,081  crore to Government sector 
which was 22.46 per cent of their total sales. 
(Para 1.4.3.1) 
 
 
Out of 757 CPSEs (including seven Statutory Corporations) under the audit jurisdiction of CAG as 
on 31 March 2024, the financial Statements for the year 2023 -24 were received from 607 CPSEs 
by 30 September 2024. The CAG reviewed financial statements of 327 CPSEs (including seven 
Statutory Corporations).  
The financial impact of significant comments, issued by the CAG on the financial statements of the 
selected CPSEs, on profitability and assets/ liabilities was ₹3,563.37 crore and ₹61,949.59 crore 
respectively. A few companies viz. the Dredging Corporation of India Limited, Oriental Insurance

The review of Corporate Governance covered 65 listed CPSEs, whose shares were listed on stock 
exchanges (including 22 CPSEs whose both shares and bonds/debentures were listed) and 36 
CPSEs/Statutory Corporations (including four Statutory Corporations namely National Highways 
Authority of India, Inland Waterways Authority of India, Food Corporation of India and National 
Cooperative Development Corporation), whose only bonds/debentures were listed on stock 
exchanges during the period from 01 April 2023 to 31 March 2024 under the administrative control 
of various Ministries. It was observed that the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, Guidelines 
of Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) and Regulations of Securities and Exchange Board of 
India (SEBI) regarding Corporate Governance were not being complied with by some of the CPSEs/ 
Statutory Corporations, as brought out below. 
 
          (Para 3.1.2) 
 
The review of composition of the Board of Directors during the year 2023 -24 revealed that 58 of 
65 listed CPSEs had the required number (at least 50 per cent of the total Board strength) of Non-
Executive Directors, while seven CPSEs did not meet this requi rement for periods ranging from 
two months to 12 months. Further, the required number of Independent Directors were not on the 
Board in 49 CPSEs (75 per cent) for periods ranging from one month to 12 months (percentage of 
shortfall ranged between 13 to 100 per cent).  
 
(Para 3.2.1 and 3.2.2) 
 
Fifty-eight of 65 listed CPSEs had a Woman Director on the Board, while seven CPSEs (11 per 
cent), did not have Woman Director on the Board for periods ranging from two to 12 months during 
2023-24. Further, Regulation 17 (1) (a) of SEBI (Listing Obligation and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulation, 2015 stipulated that Board of directors of the top 1000 listed entities shall have at least 
one independent woman director. However, 16 listed CPSEs (out of 60 CPSEs part of to p 1,000 
listed entities) did not have Woman Independent Director on the Board for periods ranging from 
two to 12 months during 2023-24. 
                                                                                                                        
(Para 3.2.3) 
 
SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 stipulate that Board of 
Directors of the top 2,000 listed entities shall comprise not less than six Directors. Review of the 
composition of the Board of Directors revealed that this criteria was not met in five CPSEs (out of 
62 CPSEs part of top 2,000 listed entities).

of Board of Directors, Board Committee of which they are members and General Meetings of the 
company. Audit observed that Independent Directors of two CPSEs (three per cent) of 65 listed 
CPSEs did not attend at least 80 per cent meetings of the Board and i ts Committees during 2023-
24. Further, Independent Directors of six CPSEs (nine per cent) did not attend General meetings of

(Para 3.3.1 and 3.3.2) 
  
Section 203 (4) of Companies, Act 2013 stipulates that if the office of any whole -time ke y 
managerial personnel is vacated, the resulting vacancy shall be filled -up by the Board within a 
period of six months from the date of such vacancy. However, in 12 CPSEs (18 per cent) of 65 
listed CPSEs, vacancy of whole time key managerial personnel was not filled within a period of six 
months. The delay ranged from five months to 37 months beyond the stipulated time frame.  
                                                                                                                      
(Para 3.4) 
  
Audit Committee was not constituted in one CPSEs (two per cent); at least two-thirds of the Audit 
Committee members were not Independent Directors in four CPSEs (six per cent ); Audit 
Committee Chairperson did not attend AGM in two CPSEs (three per cent ). A udit Committee 
quorum was insufficient in five CPSEs (eight per cent).   
 
 (Para 3.6.1.1, 3.6.1.2, 3.7 and 3.6.3) 
 
Recommendation: 
The Administrative Ministries/Departments may ensure compliance with provisions of 
Companies Act, 2013, SEBI regulations and DPE guidelines on Corporate Governance so as to 
achieve the objectives of Corporate Governance in listed CPSEs/Statutory Corporations. Board 
of Directors/Management of such listed entities may also ensure compliance of the requirements 
on Corporate Governa nce so as to bring better transparency and accountability in their 
functioning.  
 
          
 
The Chapter has covered expenditure on Research and Development activities by 26 selected Ratna 
category CPSEs during the period 2019-20 to 2023-24. Audit noted that CPSEs were not bound to 
frame dedicated and uniform policy for taking up Research and Development activities, in the 
absence of any Government guidelines. 
Out of 26 CPSEs selected for audit, more  than half of them did not have dedicated policy and 
instead followed Quality policy/ Action plans/ other related guidelines/ framework documents etc. 
                                      
(Para 4.5.1) 
 
During 2021-22 to 2023-24, 9-13 CPSEs (Maharatna, Navratna and Miniratna) incurred less than 
2 per cent of Profit Before Tax on Research and Development, whereas, three CPSEs (one Navratna 
and two Miniratna) did not incur any Research and Development expenditure during this period.  
              
(Para 4.5.2.2) 
Although majority of the selected Ratna CPSEs had well defined mechanism in place for 
implementation of Research and Development projects, there was lack of effective monitoring of 
IV.  Expenditure in Research and Development by CPSEs 
 
 
 
 
 
Research and Development projects. Out of 26 CPSEs only 13 had Apex/ Review/Sub-committee 
for periodic monitoring of Research and Development activities.         
 (Para 4.5.4)  
There were substantial delays ranging between 1 -69 months in completion of Research and 
Development projects. Out of 6,783 projects taken up by 22 C PSEs during 2019 -20 to 2023 -24, 
5,816 projects were completed, including 1652 projects completed beyond scheduled completion 
date besides 172 that were ongoing but delayed.                          
(Para 4.5.3.1) 
Twelve out the 26 selected CPSEs generated revenue of ₹33,977.35 crore through 
commercialisation of R&D activities. 1,670 research papers were got published by 16 CPSEs and 
10 CPSEs had not published any research papers. Further, out of 2,436 patents filed for registration 
by 17 CPSEs, 952 patents were granted 1466 patent applications were under process while 18 were 
rejected.                  
(Para 4.5.6.1, 4.5.6.2 and 4.5.7) 
Recommendation: 
 Government may consider developing dedicated policy/guidelines on Research and Deve
lopment activities for CPSEs. 
 Mechanisms should be put in place to ensure better monitoring, execution and evaluatio
n of Research and Development projects to ensure timely completion and to achieve the 
envisaged impact.  
 CPSEs should be encouraged to recognize the strategic impo rtance of R&D through 
regular workshops, webinars, and incentives to drive innovation, improve 
competitiveness, and contribute to long-term business success. 
 
 
The review covered 58 CPSEs (10 Maharatna, 12 Navratna, 18 Miniratna and 18 others) under the 
administrative control of various Ministries/ Departments. The period of one year ended March 
2024 was covered during the review in respect of 58s CPSEs.  
The following significant observations were made in the review:  
Five CPSEs (NFDCL, SDCL, JKDFCL, IL, NERAMAC) did not constitute CSR committee.  
NFDCL and SDCL were not required to form CSR Committee as per provisions of Companies Act 
2013. Whereas JKDFCL, IL and NERAMAC were below five crores slab of net profit hence CSR 
was not applicable. In case of CONCOR only two directors were on CSR committee. Eight CPSEs 
did not frame CSR policy duly approved by the Board. Eighteen CPSEs did not formulate Annual 
Action Plan.  
 
(Para 5.3.1, 5.3.2, 5.3.3) 
 
Total spend on CSR activities by 58 CPSEs in FY 2023 -24 was ₹3,339.80 crore. There was short 
fall in CSR expenditure reported by 15 CPSEs. The Petroleum and Power sector spent accounted 
for 69 per cent of the total CSR spend. Three CPSEs ONGC, IOCL and PGCIL accounted for 42.60 
per cent of total CSR expenditure.

Out of 58 CPSEs, 18 CPSEs were having unspent amount of ₹517.48 crore at the  end of financial 
year 2023 -24. These eighteen CPSEs transferred the remaining unspent CSR budget to either 
Unspent CSR Account or to a fund specified under Schedule VII as per section 135(5) of the 
Companies Act, 2013 within the prescribed time. Out of th ese 18 CPSEs, four CPSEs transferred 
the unspent amount to both Unspent CSR Account and to specified fund under Schedule VII.
    
(Para 5.4.4) 
Twenty nine  CPSEs incurred ₹112.03 crore towards administrative overhead and 20 CPSEs 
incurred ₹7.47 crore on Impact Assessment during 2023-24. CSR spend was mainly concentrated 
towards activities relating to Healthcare & Nutrition during the period 2023-24. 26 out of 58 CPSEs, 
could not achieve the target of 60 per cent to be spent on common theme “Health & Nutrition ” 
during 2023-24. 37 CPSEs incurred CSR expenditure (₹277.20 crore) in Aspirational Districts on 
a common theme which is 8.30 per cent of total CSR expenditure. 
(Para 5.4.5 and 5.4.6) 
Eight CPSEs did not conduct baseline survey/need assessment studies in r espect of 198 
projects/activities.    
(Para 5.5.1) 
Out of 58 CPSEs, four CPSEs undertook in -house projects only , six CPSEs outsourced all CSR 
projects to external agencies , 32 CPSEs have undertaken both in -house projects as well as 
outsourced CSR projects to external agencies.         
(Para 5.5.2) 
Thirteen CPSEs did not define Local Area in their CSR policy and eight CPSEs did not give 
preference to local area.  
(Para 5.5.4) 
Five CPSEs did not disclose the CSR activities on the website. Seven CPSEs did not comply with 
the disclosure format while reporting on CSR activities in their Annual Report as prescribed by the 
Companies (CSR Policy) Amendment Rules, 2022 (rule 5-Annexure II). 
(Para 5.7.1 and 5.7.2) 
 
 
Audit carried out analysis of MoU between six Navratna CPSEs and their respective Administrative  
Ministries for the years 2022-23 and 2023-24. Audit observed that: 
In the MoU guidelines issued by DPE, no timelines were mentioned for holding of Inter Ministerial 
Committee (IMC) meeting to finalise the MoU parameters. The time taken for signing the MoU 
from holding the IMC meeting ranged between 27 and 75 days for 2022 -23 in fiv e out of six 
selected CPSEs and between 24 and 56 days in five out of six selected CPSEs for 2023-24. 
(Para 6.5.1.1) 
VI.  Analysis of MoU between Administrative Ministries and Navratna CPSEs    
 
 
 
 
 
In respect of five out of six selected CPSEs, Ministries did not prepare and upload Sectoral Vision 
Plan on MoU dashboard for finalisation of MoU targets for 2022-23 and 2023-24. 
(Para 6.5.1.2) 
No timelines were fixed for finalization and uploading of MoU in DPE guidelines; resultantly there 
was delay in signing of MoU in respect of EIL and NMDC for 2022-23.  
(Para 6.5.1.3) 
In case of EIL, th e MoU with its subsidiary CEIL for the year 2023 -24 was signed almost at the 
end of financial year 2023 -24 thereby leaving very little time with the subsidiary to achieve the 
targets. Further, in case of Shipping Corporation of India (SCI), there was delay of nine months and 
two months in granting exemption to its subsidiary Inland Coastal Shipping Limited from signing 
MoU for the years 2022-23 and 2023-24 respectively.  
 (Para 6.5.1.4) 
Despite non-compliance of the provisions of SEBI (LODR) Regulations on Corporate Governance 
viz., minimum number of Independent Directors/ Independent Woman Directors, the 
Administrative Ministries and DPE did not deduct marks from the MoU score of CPSEs as required 
in MoU Guidelines. 
(Para 6.5.2.1) 
In respect of EIL and SCI,  no specific target for MoU compliance parameter ‘Health and Safety 
improvement of Human Resources in CPSE’ was fixed by the concerned Administrative Ministries 
for 2022-23 and 2023-24. However, DPE mentioned compliance with this parameter and did not 
deduct any mark in the MoU evaluation report for 2022-23 and 2023-24. 
(Para 6.5.2.3) 
The compliance Parameter “Target as given by NITI Aayog on Assets Monetization Milestone” 
was removed from the DPE portal/dashboard during MoU evaluation despite this parameter being 
part of the signed MoUs. 
(Para 6.5.2.4) 
The CPSEs were required to upload the estimated figures of certain financial and physical attributes 
on MoU dashboard by 31 December 2021 and 31 December 2022 for MoU years 2022 -23 and 
2023-24 respectively. However, Audit observed that the estimated figures were uploaded by the six 
selected CPSEs with a delay of 87 to 104 days and 55 to 76 days for 2022 -23 and 2023 -24 
respectively. 
 (Para 6.5.3.1) 
DPE had taken considerable time ranging from 55 to 100 days for the year 2022-23 and from 68 to 
92 days for the year 2023-24 in awarding final ranking/ score in respect of six selected CPSEs. 
(Para 6.5.3.2)

2023-24 respectively. However, Audit observed that the estimated figures were uploaded by the six 
selected CPSEs with a delay of 87 to 104 days and 55 to 76 days for 2022 -23 and 2023 -24 
respectively. 
 (Para 6.5.3.1) 
DPE had taken considerable time ranging from 55 to 100 days for the year 2022-23 and from 68 to 
92 days for the year 2023-24 in awarding final ranking/ score in respect of six selected CPSEs. 
(Para 6.5.3.2)

The Department of Investment and Public A sset Management (DIPAM) realised an amount  
of ₹16,507.29 crore during the year 2023-24 through disinvestment (Initial Public Offer, Offer for

(Para 7.5) 
Target and achievement for disinvestment 
The Budget Estimate for receipts through disinvestment for the year 2023 -24 was fixed by the 
Department of Economic Affairs (DEA) at ₹51,000 crore. However, no specific estimates for 
disinvestment were made in the Revised Estimates for the year 2023-24. The actual disinvestment 
receipts during the year 2023-24 were ₹16,507.29 crore. 
(Para 7.4) 
 Dividend income treated as disinvestment receipt 
The Specified Undertaking of Unit Trust of India (SUUTI) remitted (March 2024) dividend income 
of ₹1,770 crore to DIPAM which was reported by DIPAM as part of the Disinvestment receipts for 
the year 2023-24 (Annual Report). Since the dividend income is not a part of remittance from sale 
of Government Shareholdings, it should not be included in disinvestment receipts.  
{Para7.6.5 (a)} 
Sale of Government’s shareholding in Axis Bank Limited  
Disinvestment receipts of ₹40.32 crore from the sale of shares of Axis Bank Limited were remitted 
(3 April 2023) by the Specified Undertaking of Unit Trust of India (SUUTI) to DIPAM, which 
were booked under the head ‘Other receipts in Government Account’ i nstead of the head 
‘Disinvestment of public sector and other undertakings’. This resulted in incorrect booking of 
disinvestment receipts from the sale of shares of Axis Bank Limited.   
{Para 7.6.5 (b)} 
 
 
SEBI (July 2023) introduced the BRSR Core framework to strengthen assurance and enhance 
Environment, Social, and Governance disclosure requirements for listed entities. As per the 
regulations, for the financial year 2023 -24, the top 1000 listed companies i n India by market 
capitalization as of March 31, 2024 were required to include BRSR disclosures in their Annual 
Reports. Additionally, the top 150 entities are required to obtain reasonable assurance for the BRSR 
Core disclosures to ensure accuracy and credibility. Audit reviewed disclosures made by 30 CPSEs 
based on market capitalization for the year ended March 2024.  
BRSR framework issued by SEBI is divided in three sections comprising of 145 indicators.  
  Section A: General Disclosure (26 indicators): Captures basic information about the entity. 
  Section B: Management and Process Disclosure (12 indicators). 
  Section C: Principle-wise Performance Disclosure 
VII.  Disinvestment Process 
VIII.  Review of Sustainability Status 
 
 
 
 
 
Section C is divided into nine principles seeking disclosure on the performance of entity. Nine 
principles are divided into 68 essential indicators and 39 leadership indicators. Essential indicators 
were required to be reported on a mandatory basis, while leadership indicators were voluntary. 
Highlights of the observations noticed during Audit are as under:   
 Entities were required to disclose its paid -up capital. While reporting, paid -up capital for 
2022-23 was disclosed by one entity instead of 2023-24.  
(Para 8.5.1) 
 Entities were required to disclose reporting boundary i.e. whether the reporting was made on 
standalone basis or on consolidated basis. Though reporting boundary was “consolidated 
basis”, details of all the subsidiaries, JVs, associates etc. were not considered. 
(Para 8.5.1) 
 Entities were required to disclose gender wise segregated details of its total employees and 
workers, under permanent and other than permanent category including differently abled 
persons in each category. There were inconsistencies in disclosure viz. no gender segregation, 
no details for differently abled persons etc. 
(Para 8.5.1) 
 Entities were required to map the National/International codes/certifications adopted. 
Though, CPSE disclosed that codes/standards etc. have been adopted, suc h codes/standards 
were not available with the entity. Mapping was also not done by the CPSEs. 
(Para 8.5.2) 
 Entities were required to disclose specific commitment/target with defined timelines and 
corresponding achievements against that. Disclosed targets l acked measurability/defined 
timelines and achievements reported were not specific and of general nature. 
(Para 8.5.2) 
 Entities were required to disclose details of purchases, sales, loans, investment with related 
parties. Despite having transactions with related parties, information was disclosed as ‘Nil’. 
(Para 8.5.3.1) 
 There were instances for incorrect/deficient disclosure in respect of coverage for health & 
accidental insurance, maternity/paternity benefits, coverage under retirement benefits. 
(Para 8.5.3.3) 
 There were instances for non -disclosure for weblinks in various instances viz. grievance 
redressal policy for stakeholders, equal opportunity policy, cyber security policy. 
(Para 8.5.1, 8.5.3.3 and 8.5.3.9)

A Government company is defined in Section 2(45) of 
the Companies Act, 2013 as a company in which not 
less than 51 per cent of the paid -up share capital is 
held by Central Government, or by any State 
Government or Governments, or partly by the Central 
Government and partly by one or more State 
Governments, and includes a company which is a 
subsidiary of a Government company. 
Besides, any other company 1 owned or controlled, 
directly or indirectly, by the Central Government, or by any State Government or Gove rnments, or 
partly by the Central Government and partly by one or more State Governments are referred to in this 
Report as Government controlled other companies.  
This chapter of the Report presents the summary of financial performance of Government companies, 
Statutory Corporations and Government controlled other companies. In the Report, the term Central 
Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) encompasses those Government companies in which the direct 
holding of the Central Government is 50 per cent  or more and  subsidiary of such Government 
companies. The Statutory Corporations set up under Statutes enacted by the Parliament and other 
companies owned or controlled, directly or indirectly by the Central Government have also been 
categorised as CPSEs. 
Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) stated (December 2024) in its Public Enterprises Survey 2023-
24 that CPSEs meant those Government companies, besides Statutory Corporations, wherein more than 
50 per cent equity is held by the Central Government.   
The subsidiaries of these companies, if registered in India, are also categorised as CPSEs. It does not 
cover departmentally run public enterprises, banking institutions and insurance companies. 
                                                           
1 Companies (Removal of Difficulties) Seventh Order, 2014 issued by Ministry of Corporate Affairs vide Gazette 
Notification dated 04 September, 2014. 
PREFACE CHAPTER I 
Summary of Financial Performance of

1.1 Introduction 
Government Company 
Any company in which not less than 51 
per cent of paid-up share capital is held 
by Central Government or by one or 
more State Governments or partly by 
Central Government and partly by State 
Government(s) and includes subsidiary 
of a Government company. 

 
 
 
2 
 
In view of difference in definition adopted by the Comptroller and Auditor  General of India (CAG) 
and DPE, there was difference in number of companies considered as CPSEs by CAG and by DPE. 
As a result, the number of CPSEs as per DPE’s Public Enterprises Survey 2023-24 was 448 whereas 
the number of CPSEs as per this Report was 7 57 (528 Government companies and Statutory 
Corporations and 229 Government controlled other companies). 
1.1.1 Mandate 
Audit of Government companies and Government controlled other companies is conducted by the 
CAG under the provisions of Section 143(5) to 143(7) of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Section 
19 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 and the Regulations made 
thereunder. Under the Companies Act, 2013, the CAG appoints the Chartered Accountants as 
Statutory Auditors for Government companies and Government controlled other companies and gives 
directions on the manner in which the accounts of such companies are to be audited. In addition, CAG 
has the right to conduct a supplementary audit. The statutes governing some Statutory Corporations 
require their accounts to be audited only by the CAG. 
The Acts governing Reserve Bank of India, Export -Import Bank of India, National Bank for 
Agricultural and Rural Development and National Housing Bank contain provisions whereby the 
Central Government can appoint the CAG, at any time, as the auditor to examine and report upon the 
accounts of these institutions. No such appointment was made till 2023-24. 
1.1.2 What this Report contains 
This Report gives an overall picture of the financial performance of the CPSEs as revealed from their 
accounts. 
Impact of revision of financial statements as well as significant comments issued as a result of 
supplementary audit of the financial statements of the CPSEs conducted by the CAG for the year 
2023-24 (and of earlier years which were finalised during the current year) is given in this Report. 
This Report also contains the impact of comments issued by the CAG on the financial statements of 
the Statutory Corporations where CAG is the sole auditor.  
This Report also gives an overall picture of the status of the adherence of CPSEs to the guidelines 
issued by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), DPE and compliance with provisions 
of the Companies Act, 2013 on Corporate Governance, Corporate Social Responsibility, Analysis of 
Memoradum of Understanding and Review of sustainability status in Listed CPSEs (Business 
Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting) along with  review of Disinvestment in CPSEs and 
Expenditure in Research & Development by CPSEs.

   1.2.2.3 Interest Coverage Ratio 
Interest coverage ratio (ICR) is used to determine the ability of a company to pay interest on 
outstanding debt and is calculated by dividing a company’s Earnings Before Interest and Taxes 
(EBIT) by interest expenses of the same period. A higher ICR signifies that a company can 
comfortably meet its interest obligations, indicating financial stability, while a lower ratio suggests a 
higher risk of financial distress and potential difficulty in servicing debt.   The details of positive and 
negative interest coverage ratio of CPSEs, which had outstanding loans, during the last three years

 1.2.4 Market capitalisation of equity investment in Government companies 
Market capitalisation represents market value of the shares of companies whose shares are listed.  As 
on 31 March 2024, shares of 79 CPSEs consisting o f 60 Government companies, 11 subsidiaries 15 of 
Government companies and eight Government controlled other companies 16 were listed on various 
stock exchanges in India.  Three of these CPSEs (BEML Land Assets Limited, Shipping Corporation 
of India Land and Assets Limited and Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Limited) got 
listed during 2023 -24. Further, out of 11 subsidiaries of Government companies, the shares of two 
subsidiary companies were listed in Calcutta Stock Exchange17. 
The shares of 60 Government companies and nine subsidiaries of Government companies ( excluding two 
companies which were listed in Calcutta Stock Exchange) were traded on the BSE during 2023-24. 
The total market value of shares of 66 traded listed Government companies (Annexure V) (including 
nine subsidiary companies and excluding 3 newly listed CPSEs during the year) stood at ₹37,92,736 
crore (equity investment being ₹1,23,962 crore) as on 31 March 2024 as compared to ₹17,28,066 crore 
(equity investment was ₹1,17,689 crore) of 66 CPSEs as on 31 March 2023.  Thus, the total market 
value of shares of traded listed CPSEs increased by ₹20,64,670 crore (119.48 per cent) as on 31 March 
2024. 
The market value of GOI shares in these 66 traded listed Government companies (including nine 
subsidiary companies) stood at ₹23,51,459 crore as on 31 March 2024 as compared to ₹10,50,225 
crore in 66 CPSEs as on 31 March 2023.  Thus, the market value of GOI shares of traded listed 
CPSEs increased by ₹13,01,234 crore (123.90 per cent) as on 31 March 2024. 
Keeping in view the definition18 of Large Cap, Mid Cap and Small Cap as prescribed by SEBI and 
the market capitalization value of top 500 listed companies as per BSE, the 69 traded listed CPSEs 
have been categorised into Large Cap, Mid Cap and Small Cap as given in Table 1.8.

1.3.3  Erosion of capital in CPSEs 
1.3.3.1   Erosion of capital in Government companies 
As on 31 March 2024 there were 214 Government companies28 with accumulated losses of ₹2,47,181 
crore.  Of the 214 CPSEs, 152 CPSEs incurred loss in the year 2023-24 amounting to ₹25,972 crore 
and 62 CPSEs had not incurred loss (including zero profit/loss companies) in the year 2023-24, even 
though they had accumulated losses of ₹1,29,274 crore.  Ni neteen out of 214 CPSEs were under 
closure as on 31 March, 2024 with accumulated losses of ₹5,690 crore. 
Overall, net worth of all the 479 Government companies and corporations was ₹31,23,174 crore 
against their paid -up capital of ₹14,40,927 crore.  Net wo rth of 91 out of 214 CPSEs had been 
completely eroded by accumulated losses and their net worth was either zero or negative. The net 
worth of these 91 CPSEs was (-) ₹58,175 crore against equity investment of ₹25,103 crore as on 31 
March 2024 (Annexure-VIII). This included seven listed companies whose net worth was (-) ₹24,172 
crore against equity investment of ₹1,047 crore.  Out of 91 CPSEs whose capital had been eroded 
(being zero or negative net worth), 21 CPSEs had earned profit of ₹961 crore during 2023 -24.  
Further, 37 out of 91  CPSEs had incurred losses continuously during last five years and the 
accumulated loss and negative net worth as on 31 March 2024 amounted to ₹62,801 crore and 
₹44,330 crore respectively. 
In 16 out of 91 CPSEs whose capital had eroded, Government loans outstanding as on 31 March 2024 
amounted to ₹7,336 crore. This included two listed companies (Madras Fertilizers Limited and 
Scooters India Limited) with outstanding Government loans of ₹1,487 crore. 
Net worth was less than half of  their paid-up capital in respect of 36 out of 386 CPSEs whose net 
worth was positive at the end of 31 March, 2024.  Out of 36 CPSEs, 8 CPSEs with net worth of 
₹13,914 crore were incurring continuous losses during last five years and 19 CPSEs with net wort h 
of ₹4,799 crore were incurring losses for two to four years in the last five years indicating their 
potential financial sickness.  
1.3.3.2  Erosion of capital in Government controlled other companies 
As on 31 March, 2024 there were 49 Government controlled other companies with accumulated losses 
of ₹5,250 crore. Of the 49 CPSEs, 29 CPSEs incurred loss in the year 2023-24 amounting to ₹635 
crore and 20 CPSEs earned profits in the year 2023-24, even though they had accumulated losses of 
₹2,326 crore.

1.4.1 Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) 
Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) is a ratio that measures a company’s profitability and efficiency 
with which its capital is employed. ROCE is calculated by dividing a company’s earnings before 
interest and taxes (EBIT) by the capital employed30. The CPSE wise details of ROCE are given in 
Annexure X. The consolidated ROCE of all the CPSEs 31 during last three years from 2021 -22 to 
2023-24 is given in Table 1.17.

CHAPTER II 
Oversight Role of CAG 

 
 
 
24 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
25 
 
 
 
 
 
Comptroller & Auditor General of India (CAG) appoints the statutory auditors of a Government 
company and Government controlled other company under Section 139 (5) and (7) of the Companies 
Act, 2013. CAG has a right to conduct a supplementary audit and issue comments upon or supplement 
the Audit Report of the statutory auditor.  Statutes governing some corporations require that their 
financial statements be audited by the CAG and a report be submitted to the Parliament. 
Section 139 (5) of the Companies Act, 2013 provides that the 
statutory auditors in case of a Government company or 
Government controlled other company are to be appointed by 
the CAG within a period of 180 days from the commencement 
of the financial year.  The statutory auditors of these Public 
Sector Enterprises for the year 2023-24 were appointed by the 
CAG in September 2023. 
 
2.3.1 Need for timely submission 
According to Section 394 of the Companies Act, 2013, Annual Report on the working and affairs of 
a Government company is to be prepared within three months of its Annual General Meeting (AGM).  
As soon as possible, after such preparation, the Annual Report must be laid before both th e Houses 
of Parliament, together with a copy of the Audit Report and comments of the CAG upon or as 
supplement to the Audit Report.  Almost similar provisions exist in the respective Acts regulating 
Statutory Corporations.  This mechanism provides the nece ssary parliamentary oversight over the 
utilisation of public funds invested in the companies/statutory corporations from the Consolidated 
Fund of India. 
Section 96 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires every company to hold AGM of the shareholders 
once in every calendar year.  It is also stated that not more than 15 months shall elapse between the 
date of one AGM and that of the next.  The section further provides that in case of the first annual

financial year of the company and in any other case, within a period of six months, from the date of 
closing of the financial year.  The section also stipulates that the Registrar may, for any special reason, 
extend the time within which any annual general meeting, other than the first annual general meeting, 
shall be held, by a period not exceeding three months. 
Further, Section 129 of the Companies Act, 2013 stipulates that the audited Financial Statement for 
the financial year has to be placed in the said AGM for their consideration. The section also provides 
for levy of penalty like fine and imprisonment on the persons including Directors of the company 
responsible for non-compliance with the provisions of Section 129 of the Companies Act, 2013.

  2.4.1 Financial reporting framework  
Companies are required to prepare the financial statements in the format laid down in Schedule III to 
the Companies Act, 2013 and in adherence to the mandatory Accounting Standards prescribed by the 
Central Government, in consultation with National Financial Reporting Authority. The Statutory 
Corporations are required to prepare their financial statements in the format prescribed under the 
rules, framed in consultation with the CAG and/or any other specific provision relating to account s 
in the Act governing such corporations.

2.4 CAG’s oversight - Audit of financial statements 

 
 
 
28 
2.4.2 Audit of financial statements of Public Sector Enterprises by Statutory Auditors  
The statutory auditors appointed by the CAG under Section 139 of the Companies Act, 2013, conduct 
audit of financial statement s of the Government companies and submit their report thereon in 
accordance with the provisions of Section 143 of the Companies Act, 2013.  
The CAG plays an oversight role by monitoring the performance of the statutory auditors in audit of 
public sector undertakings with the overall objective that the statutory auditors discharge the functions 
assigned to them properly and effectively.  This function is discharged by exercising the power to: 
 issue directions to the statutory auditors under Section 143 (5) of the Companies Act, 2013 and 
 supplement or comment upon the Statutory Auditors’ report under Section 143 (6) of the 
Companies Act, 2013. 
2.4.3 Supplementary audit of financial statements of Public Sector Enterprises  
The prime responsibility for preparati on of financial statements in accordance with the financial 
reporting framework prescribed under the Companies Act, 2013 or other relevant Act is of the 
management of an entity.  
The statutory auditors appointed by the CAG under section 139 of the Companies Act, 2013 are 
responsible for expressing an opinion on the financial statements under section 143 of the Companies 
Act, 2013 based on an independent audit in accordance with the Standard Auditing Practices of 
Institute of Chartered Accountants of  India (ICAI) and directions given by the CAG.  The statutory 
auditors are required to submit the Audit Report to CAG under Section 143 of the Companies Act, 
2013. 
The certified financial statements of selected Public Sector Enterprises along with the repo rt of the 
statutory auditors are reviewed by CAG by carrying out a supplementary audit.  Based on such 
review, significant audit observations, if any, are reported under Section 143 (6) of the Companies 
Act, 2013 to be placed before the AGM.

2.5.1 Audit of the financial statements of CPSEs under Section 143 of the Companies Act, 2013  
and Audit of Statutory Corporations as per their respective Acts 
Financial statements for the year 2023-24 were received from 418 Government companies (including 
67 listed companies), 182 Government controlled other companies (including eight listed companies) 
and seven Statutory Corporations by 30 September 2024.  Of these, financial statements of 235 
Government companies and 85 Government controlled other companies an d seven Statutory 
Corporations were reviewed in audit by the CAG. 
In total, CAG reviewed f inancial statements of 56.22 per cent of 
the Government companies and 46.70 per cent  of G overnment 
controlled other companies out of the f inancial statements  
received up to 30 September 2024.  The results of the review are 
detailed below: 
Significant comments of the CAG  
Subsequent to the aud it of the financial statements by statutory auditors, the CAG conducted 
supplementary audit of the financial statements of the selected CPSEs.  The list of 107 CPSEs in respect 
of whom comments were issued is given in Annexure XII.   Summary of some of the significant 
comments issued on financial statements of CPSEs, the financial impact of which on the profitability 
was ₹3,563.37 crore and on assets/ liabilities was ₹61,949.59 crore, have been given below.   
a. Listed Government CPSEs 
a. i. Comments on Profitability 
Sl. 
No. 
Name of the 
CPSE 
Comment 
1.  Coal India 
Limited 
Coal India Limited (CIL) had given ₹57.42 crore as advance to CMPDIL for 14 R&D 
projects completed during 2022-23 and 2023-24. As per Paragraph 54 of Ind AS 38, 
research expenditure should be expensed when incurred; however, CIL did not adjust 
the advances against the R&D expenses, resulting in understatement of Other 
Expenses and overstatement of Profit by ₹57.42 crore, with a corresponding 
overstatement of Other Current Assets. 
2.5 Result of CAG’s oversight role 
CAG reviewed financial 
statements of 320 CPSEs and 
seven Statutory Corporations 
for the year 2023-24. 

 
 
 
31 
Sl. 
No. 
Name of the 
CPSE 
Comment 
2.  IFCI Limited Impairment Loss Allowance for FY 2023 -24 has been understated and profit 
overstated by a total of ₹249.97 crore. IFCI had several stressed loan accounts where 
provisions were short-created. In the case of Gran Electronics Pvt. Ltd., against an 
outstanding principal of ₹135.81 crore, provision for only ₹97.24 crore was created, 
resulting in a shortfall of ₹38.57 crore. Similarly, in Videocon Industries Ltd., 
recoverable dues were limited to ₹74.71 crore as per the NCLT-approved resolution 
plan, requiring a provision of ₹307.02 crore against which only ₹219.83 crore was 
created, leading to a shortfall of ₹87.19 crore. 
 
Further, under-provisioning was noted in other major accounts including Pioneer 
Gas Power Ltd. (shortfall ₹56.12 crore),  Liz Traders & Agents Pvt. Ltd. (shortfall 
₹22 crore), Arcotech Ltd. (shortfall ₹4.99 crore), C & C Projects Ltd. (shortfall ₹8.58 
crore), Madhucon Infrastructure Ltd. (shortfall ₹28.54crore), and Asian Colour 
Coated Ispat Ltd. (shortfall ₹3.98 crore). These short-provisions collectively resulted 
in profit overstatement and impairment loss allowance understatement by the same 
amount. 
 
It is pertinent to note that these issues were repeatedly pointed out during FY 2020-
21, 2021-22, and 2022-23 (wherever applicable), yet no corrective action was taken 
by the Company, leading to continued misstatement of financial results. 
3.  NMDC Steel 
Limited 
Amount received from NMDC Limited towards sharing of assets under a 99 -year 
MOA dated 12 February 2024 has been recognised as income for the year 2023-24. 
However, since the arrangement is in the nature of granting Right of Use and to be 
accounted as per I nd AS 116, the amount should have been treated as Deferred 
Revenue. Treating whole amount as income has resulted in non-compliance with Ind 
AS 116 and understatement of loss by ₹74.68 crore. 
4.  NTPC Limited 
 
As per Section 135(5) of the Companies Act, 2013, Rule 7(3) of the Companies (CSR 
Policy) Amendment Rules, 2021, and ICAI’s Technical Guidance on CSR 
Accounting, excess CSR spending can be carried forward only if recognized as an 
asset; otherwise, it should be charged to expense. During 2023 -24, against the 
required CSR spend of ₹337.98 crore, the Company spent ₹200.57 crore and adjusted 
₹137.41 crore from prior excess spending without creating the requisite asset, 
resulting in non-compliance and a shortfall of ₹137.41 crore. Consequently, ‘Other 
expenses’ and ‘Current liabilities – Other current liabilities’ were understated by 
₹137.41 crore each.

1.  Coal India

 Coal India Limited (CIL), holding a 26 per cent interest in an un-incorporated joint venture 
CBM project with ONGC, did not recognise ONGC’s claim of ₹17.18 crore for the period 
23/04/2013 to 28/05/2017 and incorrectly booked ₹51.13 crore (29/05/2021 to 31 /03/2024)

disclosure requirements. 
 Coal India Limited (CIL) disclosed computer software valued at ₹140.33 crore (net ₹93.90 
crore) under Note 3.4: Intangible Assets but did not specify, as required by Paragraph 118 
of Ind AS 38, whether the useful lives were indefinite or finite, the amortisation rates, or the 
methods used. This omission in Material Accounting Policy 2.11 and Note 3.4 resulted in 
deficient disclosure of intangible assets and amortisation. 
 Coal India Limited (CIL) changed its accounting policy on stripping activity with effect 
from 01.04.2022, replacing the earlier practice of adjusting excess overburden removal 
through the Ratio Variance Reserve with recognition of Stripping Activity Assets under 
Property, Plant and Equipm ent, amortised over the life of the mine. This change, applied 
retrospectively, also introduced the statement “The stripping activity asset is amortized over 
the life of the mine” in the policy. However, unlike leasehold land and intangible assets 
where am ortisation is charged in the same year, CIL deferred amortisation of stripping 
activity assets to the subsequent year, citing that benefits from advance stripping accrue only 
in the following year —yet this deviation, as well as whether amortisation is base d on the 
‘entire’ life or the ‘balance’ life of the mine, was not disclosed. Given that stripping activity 
is integral to mining operations, Ind AS 8 and Ind AS 1 require disclosure of the nature and 
reasons for such voluntary policy change, along with the  basis and method of amortisation, 
to enable users of financial statements to make informed decisions. The absence of these 
details in Material Accounting Policy No. 2.19 resulted in a significant disclosure 
deficiency.

4.  Bharat Coking 
Coal Limited 
 Bharat Coking Coal Limited (BCCL) reported Input Tax Credit (ITC) receivable of 
₹1,531.62 crore as on 31 March 2024, an amount that has been steadily accumulating 
over the years primarily due to the inverted GST structure—output GST on coal sales 
at 5 per cent while inputs attract higher rates ranging from 5 per cent  to 28 per cent. 
The situation has been compounded by the Ministry of Finance’s Notification No. 
09/2022 – Central Tax (Rate) dated 13 July 2022, which discontinued refunds on ITC, 
thereby restricting utilization of GST paid on inputs solely against GST on outputs. 
Consequently, the annual utilization of ITC has consistently fallen short of the ITC 
credited during the year, adding to the carried -forward balances from previous years, 
and creating significant uncertainty regarding its future realization. As per Ind AS 1, 
such circumstances —being a major source of estimation uncertainty with potential 
material impact on the carrying value of assets —require detailed disclosure of the 
underlying facts , assumptions, and risks to enable users of financial statements to 
make informed decisions. However, neither BCCL in the Notes to Accounts nor the 
Statutory Auditors in their report disclosed these critical details, resulting in a material 
deficiency in disclosure requirements.

24.  South Eastern 
Coalfields 
Limited 
 South Eastern Coalfields Limited (SECL) did not disclose ₹1104.95 crore relating to 
unexecuted contractual works of Haldibari UG Mine and Amgaon OCP under revenue 
commitments, though such disclosure is mandatory under Paragraph 114(d) of Ind AS 
1. Non-disclosure of these commitments resulted in deficiency in meeting disclosure 
requirements essential for users of financial statements to make informed decisions.  
 South Eastern Coalfields Limited (SECL), in line with Coal India Limited’s revised 
policy, recognized stripping activity as an asset under Property, Plant and Equipment 
from 01.04.2022 with retrospective effect and provided for its amortization over the 
life of the mine. However, unlike other assets, SECL deferred amortization of stripping 
activity assets to the following year without disclosing this deviation in its accounting 
policy. Further, the policy did not clarify whether amortization would be over  the 
entire life or the balance life of the mine. Considering the significance of stripping 
activity in mining operations, absence of such disclosures is inconsistent with Ind AS 
1 and Ind AS 8, rendering the policy deficient. 
 South Eastern Coalfields Limi ted (SECL) recognized land compensation liabilities, 
including asset compensation and R&R benefits, immediately after sanction by the 
competent authority and capitalized ₹864.50 crore during 2023-24, in line with expert 
opinion obtained by CIL. However, ot her subsidiaries accounted compensation only 
on actual payment basis, citing completion of acquisition process as the trigger for 
capitalization. Despite having an expert view, CIL and its subsidiaries have not framed 
a uniform accounting policy or disclos ure on what constitutes “acquisition of land” 
and when to recognize related liabilities, resulting in inconsistent practices across 
subsidiaries and deficiency in disclosure of compensation obligations.

crore for 195.32 hectare, though sanctioned and approved, was neither recognized nor 
disclosed in the financial statements, as WCL followed the practice of booking only 
actual payments. Despite expert opinion obtained by CIL in 2021 recommending 
recognition of provision at the time of land a cquisition, CIL and its subsidiaries have 
not adopted a uniform policy or disclosure, leading to inconsistencies in accounting 
treatment of land acquisition and compensation obligations, in deviation from Ind AS 
1 and Ind AS 37. 
 Western Coalfields Limited (WCL), in line with Coal India Limited’s revised policy, 
recognized stripping activity as an asset under Property, Plant and Equipment from 
01.04.2022 with retrospective effect and provided for its amortization over the life of 
the mine. However, unlike ot her assets, WCL deferred amortization of stripping 
activity assets to the following year without disclosing this deviation in its accounting 
policy. Further, the policy did not clarify whether amortization would be over the 
entire or balance life of the mine. Considering the significance of stripping activity in 
mining operations, absence of such disclosure is inconsistent with Ind AS 1 and Ind

4.  Pawan Hans 
Limited (2022 -
23) 
 Ind AS 36 provides that an entity shall assess at the end of each reporting period whether 
there is any indication that an asset may be impaired. If any such indication exists, the 
entity shall estimate the recoverable amount of the asset. However, the company did not 
conduct such impairment testing exercise. The statutory auditor pointed out th is 
deficiency in its report. 
The statutory auditor in its revised report under “Basis for Adverse Opinion”, para 
1 A, states that “ Keeping in view the valuation of 51 per cent stake at ₹199.92 
crores, the total valuation of the company is ₹399.84 crore. The Company’s Net 
Worth as per Financial Statement as on 31 st March 2023 is ₹ 902.55 crore. 
Considering the valuation made by Ministry of finance, as the impairment Loss 
due to Variance in net worth in comparison with valuation of the company is ₹ 
502.71 crore.” The Statutory auditor has calculated the impairment loss on the 
basis of the valuation of 51 per cent stake in Pawan Hans Limited. However, 
the statutory auditor’s observation on valuation of the Company cannot be 
considered as the basis of calculating  the impairment loss on account of 
following: 
a. The valuation of the Company is for the Company as a whole and was carried 
out for the purpose of disinvestment of the Company, whereas impairment is 
being done only on certain class of assets and not on a Company as a whole. Ind 
AS 36 (relating to impairment of assets) is not applicable on inventory, assets 
arising from construction contracts, deferred tax assets, financial assets, non -
current assets classified as held for sale.  
b. There is a considerable time gap between the valuation of the company for the 
purpose of disinvestment and approval of the financial statement for the year 
2022-23 as the former was done prior to December 2020. Moreover, as the 
process of disinvestment was annulled, the valuation done h olds no relevance. 
In view of the above, this valuation carried out for the purpose of disinvestment 
of the Company cannot be taken as the basis for working out the impairment 
loss for the fixed asset at the end of the reporting period, i.e., 2022-23. Further, 
the same is not in compliance with Para no. 9 of the Ind AS 36, which stipulates 
that “An entity shall assess at the end of each reporting period whether there is 
any indication that an asset may be impaired. If any such indication exists, the 
entity shall estimate the recoverable amount of the asset”. 
c. There is a specified methodology for calculating impairment as per Ind AS 36 
which involves determining recoverable amount, however, in the absence of 
expert valuation committee report, it cannot be conc luded that whether the 
valuation of asset has been done in accordance with the Ind AS 36.

(VRS) excepting one-fifth of the amount so paid, are treated as Deferred Revenue Expenditure 
and equally claimed as expenditure in succeeding four years , which violates AS -15 (Para 146) 
requiring immediate expensing of termination  benefits. This non -compliance has led to 
overstatement of Deferred Revenue Expenditure by ₹124.47 crore, with corresponding 
understatement of Handling Expenses (Salary of Department Labour) by ₹113.63 crore and 
Previous Year Expenses by ₹10.84 crore. 
 The Other receipts represent net interest of ₹14.79 crore on Price Support Scheme operations of 
pulses (Note C2) which has been recognized as income despite no provision for such treatment 
in the guidelines. This is inconsistent with the Accounting Standard, w hich requires revenue 

 
 
 
54 
recognition only when there is no uncertainty regarding its ultimate collection. This has resulted 
in overstatement of both income and receivables by ₹14.79 crore. Further, no corrective action 
has been taken by FCI, despite the same being highlighted in previous years. 
 The Corporation accounts for gratuity and leave encashment on a cash basis, contrary to Para 61 
of AS-15, which requires recognition of retirement benefit costs in the Statement of Profit and 
Loss.  
 The Corporation shif ted to computerized Financial Accounting Package (FAP) since financial 
year 2013-14. At the time of switch over from manual to FAP, Management decided to consider 
the date of acquisition of all existing assets as on 01.04.2013. As a result, the date of 
acquisition/place in service of the assets acquired/placed in service prior to 01.04.2013 has also 
been shown as 01.04.2013 in the Asset Book report. Resultantly balance life of these existing 
assets could not be ascertained and consequently the undercharging of depreciation could not be 
quantified in audit. As actual date of acquisition is available in manual records, the impact of this 
change in date of acquisition should have been disclosed in the accounts. 
Inland Waterways Authority of India (2022-23) 
 As per Note 12 of Schedule -2, IWAI received ₹33.88 crore from the Ministry of External 
Affairs (MEA) up to 31 March 2023 for the Kaladan Project, including ₹29.05 crore towards 
PDC fees, ₹2.11 crore towards Service Tax, ₹1.72 crore towards GST, and ₹1 crore a s 
reimbursement for hydrographic survey expenditure. Additionally, internal receipts of ₹2.95 
crore, mainly from bank interest, were generated on the project. Against the above, an 
expenditure of ₹30.25 crore has been incurred till 31 March 2023. However, IWAI has 
maintained separate books of accounts for the Kaladan Project for FY 2022 -23, and except 
for internal receipts, no impact of these transactions has been incorporated in the main 
accounts of IWAI. As a result, the figures disclosed in the financial statements cannot be fully 
vouched by Audit. This issue has been repeatedly highlighted since 2016-17, but no corrective 
action has been taken by the Management. 
Inland Waterways Authority of India (2023-24) 
 In 2023-24, Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI) received ₹1,010.50 crore as capital 
outlay under Inland Water Transport and Capital outlay on North Eastern Areas, and ₹76.50 
crore as a revenue grant for discharging interest liability on Extra Budgetary Resources/Bonds 
for IWAI; however, the nature of these grants was not disclosed in the Financial Statements 
as required by AS-12, making Note No. 17 deficient. 
 IWAI has utilized capital grant of ₹228.65 crore on Operational & Maintenance expenses and 
Personnel & Administrative expenses instead of requesting a revenue grant for this purpose 
from the Ministry. The same issue is being raised since 2016 -17, however, the same is still 
not rectified. 
 

 
 
 
55 
National Cooperative Development Corporation of India (2023-24) 
 The Corporation’s provisioning for Non -Performing Assets (NPAs) deviated from its own 
Significant Accounting Policy, which prescribes specific minimum provisioning rates based on 
asset classification—ranging from 15 per cent for sub-standard assets to 100 per cent for loss 
assets. Instead, the Corporation made a 100 per cent  provision across all NPA categories, 
resulting in an excess provision of ₹142.86 crore. This excess provisioning has caused an 
overstatement of current liabilities and provisions for do ubtful debts, thereby understating the 
surplus (excess of income over expenditure) by ₹142.86 crore. 
National Highways Authority of India (2022-23)  
 NHAI, in 2022 -23, incorrectly adjusted ₹4,650.84 crore of highway maintenance and toll 
collection expenditure (net ₹2,689.38 crore after grants and receipts) against the Capital Account 
instead of the Profit and Loss Account, understating both the year’s loss and capital by ₹2,689.38 
crore. Additionally, ₹62.50 crore deducted from plough back of toll revenue fo r creating 
electronic toll collection infrastructure—being capital expenditure—was not capitalised, leading 
to understatement of capital and assets held on behalf of GoI. The related accounting policy is 
deficient as it treats such capital assets as expenditure, an issue repeatedly raised by audit but not 
rectified. 
 An amount of ₹9,221.93 crore of Capital Reserve was incorrectly shown as a deduction from 
“Assets held on behalf of GoI” instead of under Reserves & Surplus, contrary to accounting 
principles that require capital reserves (arising from capital profits) to be shown within reserves. 
This has understated both Reserves & Surplus and Assets held on behalf of GoI by ₹9,221.93 
crore, an issue repeatedly flagged by audit but not addressed by the management. 
 Assets held on behalf of GoI include ₹25,581.70 crore of borrowing costs capitalised to 
completed and ongoing projects during 2022-23, contrary to AS 16, which requires capitalisation 
to cease once projects are ready for use. Without project -wise details, audit could not verify the 
allocation. Cumulatively, ₹1,18,545.67 crore of borrowing costs has been capitalised up to 31 
March 2023. 
 The assets include ₹ 23,197.79 crore of “interest on unutilised capital,” comprising interest on 
unutilised grants and a dvances to contractors/consultants. As per GFR 2017 Rule 230(8), such 
interest should be remitted to the Consolidated Fund of India (CFI) and not adjusted against 
future grants. NHAI earned ₹2,350.64 crore interest in 2022 -23 but did not remit it to CFI, 
understating both current liabilities (payable to GoI) and assets held on behalf of GoI. The 
relevant accounting policy is deficient and non-compliant with GFR 
 NHAI’s investments of ₹6,572.80 crore in various companies/SPVs are carried at cost, but no 
recent valuation has been done to assess any other -than-temporary decline in value as required 
under AS 13. The last valuation of loss -making subsidiaries was in 2016 -17, after which 
provisions were made. However, without updated valuations for the remaining SPVs, audit could 
not verify the correctness of the reported investment value. This issue has been repeatedly raised 
but remains unaddressed by management. 

 
 
 
56 
 Current Assets does not include an amount of ₹85.60 crore, recoverable as on 31 March 2023 
from various concessionaires, contractors and Government agencies resulting in understatement 
of ‘Claims recoverable and understatement of ‘Liability payable to GoI’ by ₹85.60 crore. 
 Due to non/short provisioning of liability, as on 31 March 2023, towards land compensation, 
amount payable to contractors/concessionaires/utility departments and Others resulted into 
understatement of Current Liabilities and Provisions by ₹792.68  crore, ‘ Assets held on behalf 
of GoI (Completed / Ongoing)’ by ₹788.85 crore and ‘Expenditure on maintenance of highways’ 
by ₹3.83 crore. 
National Highways Authority of India (2023-24)  
 As per Section 23 of the NHAI Act, 1988, the annual statement of accounts of NHAI is to be 
prepared in the format prescribed by the Government of India (GoI) in consultation with the 
Comptroller and Auditor General of India (C&AG). 
i. NHAI has disclosed “Assets held on behalf of GoI (completed & ongoing)” amounting 
to ₹10,07,532.92 crore as a separate head in its Balance Sheet, which is not in line with 
the approved format and Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP). 
Ownership of National Highways vests with GoI and NHAI is only an executing agency, 
as confirmed (January 2015) by the Solicitor General of India. The Expert Advisory 
Committee of ICAI also opined that since NHAI does not control these highways nor 
derive future economic benefits, they should not be recognized as NHAI’s assets. 
Hence, depicting them as assets without amending the NHAI Act or approved format of 
accounts (1992) is incorrect. 
ii. NHAI, instead of preparing a Profit/Loss account as per approved format, computed 
‘Net Establishment Expenditure’ (₹800.79 crore for FY 2023 -24) and transferred it to 
“Assets held on behalf of GoI” under Fixed Assets, capitalising the entire amount. This 
treatment contravenes GAAP, as revenue expenditure cannot be booked to completed 
projects and should be routed through Profit & Loss Account. Project-wise details were 
not available, preventing Audit from quantifying the impact. Significant Accounting 
Policy No. 6 is deficient in this regard. 
iii. Borrowing costs amounting to ₹25,900.33 crore have been capitalised in FY 2023 -24 
and included in “Assets held on behalf of GoI (completed & on going)” totaling 
₹10,07,532.92 crore. As per AS 16, capitalisation should cease once qualifying assets 
are ready for use; costs related to completed projects should be charged to Profit & Loss 
Account. NHAI does not maintain project-wise details, preventing Audit from verifying 
allocation of total borrowing costs (₹1,44,446 crore till 31 March 2024). 
iv. During 2023-24, NHAI incurred ₹5,812.21 crore on highway maintenance against this, 
MoRTH released ₹1,174.07 crore as grant and NHAI earned ₹128.99 crore from o ther 
receipts. Instead of routing the net expenditure (₹4,509.15 crore) through Profit & Loss 
Account, NHAI adjusted it against Shareholder’s Fund, leading to understatement of 

 
 
 
57 
both Excess of Expenditure over Income and Shareholder’s Fund by ₹4,509.15 cror e. 
This deviation, repeatedly flagged in audit, remains unresolved. 
v. Capital (Schedule 1) excludes ₹67.29 crore spent on Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) 
and Toll Management System (TMS), which NHAI deducted from “Plough back of Toll 
Revenue.” As this is a capital expenditure, it should have been capitalised, leading to 
understatement of Capital (Schedule 1) and Assets held on behalf of GoI (Schedule 5) 
by ₹67.29 crore. Significant Accounting Policy (Schedule -18, Para 8) is also deficient 
as it sets off such  expenditure against toll remittance rather than capitalizing it. No 
corrective action has been taken despite earlier audit observations.  
 Capital Reserve of ₹9,414.73 crore has been shown as a deduction from “Assets held on behalf 
of GoI” instead of being disclosed under “Reserves & Surplus,” as required since it is created 
out of capital profits. This has resulted in understatement of both Reserves & Surplus and Assets 
held on behalf of GoI by ₹9,414.73 crore. 
 Assets held on behalf of GoI included ₹27,350 .33 crore under ‘Interest on unutilized capital,’ 
representing cumulative interest earned on unutilized capital and loans/advances to contractors 
and consultants. As per GFR 2017 Rule 230(8), such interest must be remitted to the 
Consolidated Fund of India  (CFI) and not adjusted against future releases. NHAI earned 
₹4,152.54 crore as interest during 2023 -24 but did not remit it to CFI, resulting in 
understatement of Current Liabilities (Payable to GoI) and Assets held on behalf of GoI. 
Interest earned in previous years (2017-18 to 2022-23) also needs reconciliation and remittance. 
Significant Accounting Policy No. 3, which credits such interest to “Interest on unutilized 
capital,” is deficient and contravenes GFR 2017. 
 Due to non/short provisioning of liabil ity, as on 31 March 2024, towards land compensation, 
amount payable to contractors/concessionaires/utility departments and Others resulted into 
understatement of Current Liabilities and Provisions by ₹854.72  crore, ‘Assets held on behalf 
of GoI (Completed / Ongoing)’ by ₹853.30 crore and ‘Claims Recoverable’ by ₹1.42 crore. 
 
 
In exercise of the powers conferred by Section 469 of the Companies Act, 2013, read with Section 
129 (1), Section 132 and Section 133 of the said Act, the Central Government prescribes Accounting 
Standards. Besides these, the Central Government notifies Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) 
through Companies (Indi an Accounting Standards) Rules which are being amended from time to 
time. 
The statutory auditors reported that 21 CPSEs as detailed in Annexure XIII did not comply with 
mandatory Accounting Standards/ Ind AS.

One of the objectives of financial audit is to establish communication on audit matters arising from the 
audit of financial statements between the auditor and those charged with the responsibility of 
governance of the corporate entity. 
The material observations on the financial statements of CPSEs were reported as comments by the 
CAG under Section 143 (6) of the Companies Act, 2013.  Besides these comments, irregularities or 
deficiencies observed by CAG in the financial reports or in the reporting process, were also 
communicated to the management through a ‘Management Letter’ for taking corrective action. These 
deficiencies generally related to  
 application and interpretation of accounting policies and practices,  
 adjustments arising out of audit observations that could have a significant effect on the financial 
statements and  
 inadequate or non -disclosure of certain information on which management of the concerned 
PSE gave assurances that corrective action would be taken in the subsequent year.  
During the review of financial statements, CAG issued ‘Management Let ters’ to 304 CPSEs 
(Annexure XIV). 
Based on the Management Letters issued, significant improvements made by the Management of the 
CPSEs are highlighted in Annexure XV.

Corporate Governance is the application of best Management Practices, Compliance of Laws in true 
letter and spirit and adherence  to ethical standards for effective management and distribution of 
wealth and discharge of social responsibility for sustainable development of all stakeholders. 
There are several Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) and Statutory Corporations under the 
audit jurisdiction of the Comptroller & Auditor General of India (C&AG of India) whose shares 
and/or Bonds/Debentures are listed on the Stock Exchange. In the context of the policy of the 
government to grant more autonomy to the CPSEs, Corporate Govern ance has gained importance. 
Under the Maharatna Scheme, CPSEs are expected to expand their operations and become global 
giants, for which effective Corporate Governance has become imperative. 
3.1.1  Provisions governing the Corporate Governance 
The Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) and the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) 
are the major regulatory institutions for Corporate Governance initiatives in India. SEBI monitors 
and regulates Corporate Governance of Listed Companies/Statutory Corporati ons in India. The 
regulatory provisions with respect to Corporate Governance are mainly covered under the Companies 
Act 2013, SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 and 
Regulation on SEBI (Issue and Listing of Non -Convertible Securities) 2021 and Guidelines issued 
by Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) which are explained below: 
3.1.1.1 Provisions contained in the Companies Act, 2013 
The Companies Act, 2013 was enacted on 29 August 2013 replacing the Companies Act, 1956.   In 
addition, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs has also notified (31 March 2014) Companies Rules, 2014 
on Management and Administration, Appointment and Qualification of Directors, Meetings of Board 
and its powers. The Companies Act, 2013 together with t he Companies Rules provide a robust 
framework for corporate governance. The requirements, inter alia provide for:  
 Qualifications for Independent Directors along with the duties and guidelines for professional 
conduct (Sections 149 (6) & (8) and Schedule IV read with rule 5 of the Companies 
(Appointment and Qualification of Directors) Rules, 2014. 
CHAPTER III 
Corporate Governance 
3.1 Introduction

 Mandatory appointment of one -woman Director on the board of listed companies {Section 
149(1)}.   
 Mandatory establishment of certain committees like Audit Committ ee {Section 177(1)}, 
Nomination and Remuneration Committee {Section 178(1)}, and Stakeholders Relationship 
Committee {Section 178(5)}. 
 Holding of a minimum of four meetings of Board of Directors every year in such a manner 
that not more than 120 days shall  intervene between two consecutive meetings of the Board 
{Section 173(1)}. 
3.1.1.2 Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) (Listing Obligation and Disclosure 
Requirements) Regulations, 2015 
SEBI notified (02 September 2015) the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015, which came into effect from 01 December 2015. Upto March 2024, SEBI (Listing 
Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) (Amendment) Regulations, 2021 (Last amended on 
September 2023) was notified, which has been considered for this report. 
SEBI guidelines helps to institutionalize good practices of Corporate Governance in CPSEs as per 
provisions specified in Regulations 16 to 27 for both shares and Non -Convertible Securities 36 and 
other relevant and amended provision s specified in Regulations 50 to 62 are applicable for Non -
Convertible Securities only. 
3.1.1.3  SEBI (Issue and Listing of Non-Convertible Securities) Regulation, 2021 
This regulation has been effective from 16 August, 2021 and enables an institution to establish the 
good practices of Corporate Governance in CPSEs as per provisions specified for Non -Convertible 
Securities. 
3.1.1.4  DPE guidelines on Corporate Governance 
The Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) issued guidelines on Corporate Governance in 
November 1992 on the inclusion of non -official Directors on the Board of Directors. DPE issued 
further guidelines in November 2001 providing for inclusion of independent Directors on the Board 
of Directors. To bring in more transparency and accountability in the functioning of CPSEs, the Union 
Government introduced (June 2007) the guidelines on Corporate Governance for CPSEs, which were 
modified and reissued in May 2010 were made mandatory applicable to all CPSEs. The guidelines 
issued by DPE covered are as like composition of Board of Directors,  composition and functions of 
Board committees like Audit Committee, Remuneration Committee, details on subsidiary companies, 
disclosures, reports and the schedules for implementation. All references to DPE guideli nes in this 
Chapter refer to the DPE guidelines issued in May 2010 which are mandatory for all CPSEs. DPE 
has also incorporated ‘Corporate Governance’ as a performance parameter in the Memorandum of 
Understanding (MoU) of all CPSEs.

high value debt listed entity. Thus, as Regulations 16 to 27 are not mandatory for hig h value debt listed entity, the 
compliance of Regulations 16 to 27 have not been considered for non -convertible debt securities.

3.2.1  Non-Executive Director on the Board 
The Board is the most significant instrument of corporate governance. Regulation 17 (1) (a) of SEBI 
(Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 stipulates that the  Board of 
Directors of the listed entity shall have an optimum combination of executive and non -executive 
Directors with not less than 50 per cent of the Board of Directors comprising non-executive Directors. 
The review of composition of the Board of Directors revealed that the CPSEs listed in Table 3.1 did 
not have the required number (at least 50 per cent of the total Board strength) of No n-Executive 
Directors.
