3.2.2  Independent Directors 
The presence of independent representatives on the Board, competent of taking an independent view 
of the decision of the management is considered as a means of protecting the interest of shareholders. 
In terms of section 149 (4) of the Companies Act, 2013, Rule 4 of the Companies (Appointment and 
Qualification of Directors ) Rules, 2014, Regulation 17 (1) (b) of SEBI (Listing Obligations and 
Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 and Para 3.1.4 of the DPE guidelines, where the 

 
 
 
71 
Chairman of the Board is a Non-Executive Director, at least one-third of the Board should comprise 
of Independent Directors and in case the Chairman is an Executive Director, at least half of the Board 
should comprise of Independent Directors. Provided that where the regular Non -Executive 
chairperson is a promoter of the listed entity or is related to any promoter or person occupying 
management position at the Board level or at one level below the Board of Directors, at least half of 
the Board of Directors of the listed entity shall  consist of Independent Directors. As per Regulation 
16(1) (b) of SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations 2015, ‘Independent 
Director’ shall mean a Non-Executive Director, other than a nominee Director of the listed entity.  
The review of composition of the Board of Directors revealed that in 49 out of 65 listed CPSEs (75 
per cent) (Annexure XIX ), the required number of Independent Directors were not on the Board 
during the whole/part period of the year 2023 -24. The percentage of shortfall ranged between 13 to 
100 per cent. Further, the period of shortfall ranged between one to twelve months.

Company shall have at leas t one-woman Director in its Board. The SEBI Regulations, 2015 further 
stipulate Board of Directors of the top 1,000 listed entities shall have at least one Independent Woman 
Director.  The review of composition of the Board of Directors revealed that the C PSEs listed in

3.2.6  Familiarisation programme for Independent Directors 
Regulation 25 (7) of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations 2015, 
stipulate that the company shall familiarize Independent Directors with company/ industry activities, 
their roles, rights and responsibilities and any other r elevant information. Further, Schedule V C (2) 
(g) of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations 2015 stipulates that 
a web link where the details of familiarisation programme undertaken for Independent Directors was 
to be disclosed in Annual Report.  
However, in respect of one CPSE (Dredging Corporation of India Limited), where no such 
familiarisation programme for Independent Director was conducted and in respect of one CPSE (India 
Tourism Development Corporation), the details of familiarisation programme for Independent 
Directors was not disclosed in its Annual Report.

3.6.3  Quorum of Audit Committee Meetings

CPSEs/ Statutory Corporations whose Bonds/ Debentures are listed on Stock Exchanges as on 
31 March, 2024 
There were 36 CPSEs39 and Statutory Corporations under the audit jurisdiction of the C&AG of India, 
whose Bonds/Debentures were listed in the Stock Exchange in India as on 31 March, 2024. Provisions 
governing the Corporate Governance in the CPSEs/Statutory Corporations, whose Bonds/Debentures 
were listed on stock exchanges are mainly covered under the Companies Act, 2013, DPE Guidelines, 
SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 and SEBI (Issue and 
Listing of Non-Convertible Securities) Regulations, 2021. 
Review of compliance of the Corporate Governance provisions by CPSEs and Statutory 
Corporations, whose Bonds/Debentures were listed in the Stock Exchanges in India revealed the 
following non-compliances.

mandates listed entities to provide prior intimation of at least two working days (excluding the date

3.18.1 Regulation 52(1) of SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 
2015, stipulates that the listed entity shall prepare and submit un-audited or audited quarterly and year 
to date standalone financial results on a quarterly basis in the format as specified by the Board within 
45 days from the end of the quarter, other than last quarter, to the recognized stock exchange(s). 
One Statutory Corporation (Inland Waterways Authority of India) had not submitted the financial 
results with stipulated time as per above regulation.  
3.18.2 Regulation 52(2) (d) of SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 
2015, stipulates that the annual audited standalone and consolidated financial results for the financial 
year shall be submitted to the stock exchange(s) within sixty days from the end of the financial year 
along with the audit report. Provided that issuers, who  are being audited by the Comptroller and 
Auditor General of India, shall adopt the following two step process for disclosure of the annual 
audited financial results:  
(i) The first level audit shall be carried out by the auditor appointed by the Comptroller a nd 
Auditor General of India, who shall audit the financials of the listed entity and such financial 
results shall be submitted to the Stock Exchange(s) within sixty days from the end of the 
financial year.   
(ii) After the completion of audit by the CAG, the fi nancial results shall be submitted to the 
Stock exchange(s) within nine months from the end of the financial year. 
Two (six per cent) out of 36 CPSEs/Statutory Corporations listed in Table 3.32 did not submit the 
annual audited standalone and consolidated financial results to the stock exchange(s) within sixty 
days from the end of the financial year along with the audit report.

3.18.3 Regulation 52 (8) of SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations,

Regulation 60 (2) of SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) (Fifth Amendment) 
Regulations, 2021 stipulates that the listed entity shall give notice in advance of at least seven working 
days (excluding the date of intimation and the record date) to the recognised stock exchange(s) of the 
record date (for purposes of payment of interest, dividend and payment of redempt ion or repayment 
amount or for such other purposes as specified by the stock exchange) or of as many days as the stock 
exchange(s) may agree to or require specifying the purpose of the record date. However, in respect 
of one CPSE (Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited) notice of the record date was not given to 
the stock exchange within the required time. 
Regulation 58(1)(a), (b),(c), (2) & (3) of SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015 stipulate that the listed entity shall send the following documents: (a) Soft copies 
of the full annual reports to all the holders of non -convertible securities who have registered their 
email address(es) either with the listed entity or with any deposito ry, (b) hard copy of statement 
containing the salient features of all documents as specified in Section 136 of Companies Act, 2013 
and rules made thereunder to those holders of non-convertible (securities) who have not so registered, 
(C) hard copy of full annual report to those holders in non-convertible securities who request for the 
same. 
(2) The listed entity shall send the notice of all meetings of holders of non-convertible debt securities 
and holders of non-convertible redeemable preference shares specifically stating that the provisions 
for appointment of proxy as mentioned in Section 105 of the Companies Act, 2013, shall be applicable 
for such meeting. 
(3) The listed entity shall send proxy forms to holders of non -convertible debt securities and n on-
convertible redeemable preference shares which shall be worded in such a manner that holders of 
these securities may vote either for or against each resolution.

the decision of the management is widely considered as a means of protecting the interest of 
shareholders and other stakeholders. In terms of Rule 4 of the Companies (Appointment and 
Qualification of Directors) Rules, 2014, and Para 3.1.4 of the DPE guidelines, where the Chairperson 
of the Board is a non-Executive Director, at least one-third of the Board should comprise Independent 
Directors and, in case he is an Executive Director, at least half of the Board should comprise of 
Independent Directors. The review of composition of the Board of Directors revealed that the CPSEs 
listed in Table 3.33 did not have the required number of Independent Directors on their Board.

Recommendation: 
The Administrative Ministries/Departments may ensure compliance with DPE guidelines, 
SEBI regulations and provisions of Companies Act, 2013 on Corporate Governance so as to 
achieve the objectives of Corporate Governance in listed CPSEs/Statutory Corporatio ns. 
Board of Directors/Mangement of such listed entities may also ensure compliance of the 
requirements on Corporate Governance so as to bring better transparency and accountability 
in their functioning.

CHAPTER IV 
Expenditure on Research and  
Development by CPSEs

Research & Development (R&D) activities are key to technological upgradation and result in bringing 
new products and services to the marketplace and more efficient and cost-effective processes.  
The Union Budget 2024 -25 placed emphasis on innovation, research and development as key  
contributors towards India’s progress which was evident from the initiatives to support scientific and 
technological capabilities like setting up of the Anusandhan National Research Foundation, 
investments in private sector driven research, expansion of s pace economy and advancements in 
agricultural and nuclear energy research. The Government consistently increased the budget 
allocation for science and research and the amount allocated to six major scientific 
agencies/departments40 increased by 57 per cent in the budget in 2025 -26 over that in the previous 
year.  
As per survey (2022 -23) conducted by the National Science and Technology Management 
Information System (NSTMIS) under the Department of Science and Technology (DST), the Gross 
Expenditure on Researc h and Development (GERD) more than doubled from ₹60,196.75 crore to 
₹1,27,380.96 crore in the decade from 2010 -11 to 2020 -21. The study revealed that GERD was 
mainly driven by the government sector with Central Government accounting for 43.70 per cent, 
State Governments 6.70 per cent, Public Sector Industries 4.40 per cent and Institutions of Higher 
Education 8.8 per cent and the Private Industry accounting for the balance 36.40 per cent during 
2020-21. It revealed that Research and Development expenditures  incurred by Central Government 
sources came from twelve major scientific agencies as shown in the Chart below:

The survey also highlighted that Research and Development investment as a percentage of GDP was 
0.64 per cent for India. India’s ambitious vision is to become a $ 5 trillion economy through initiatives 
like “Make in India” and “Atma Nirbhar Bharat”. In the interim budget of FY 2025, the government 
also announced a corpus of one lakh crore for research and innovation in the country adopting the 
slogan ‘Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan, Jai Vigyan, Jai Anusandhan’. 
The Research and Development activities by Central Public Sector Enterprises ( CPSEs) can 
strengthen our country’s technological strength and ensure growth and creation of jobs in the country 
and also allow CPSEs to address the new challenges and opportunities in an increasingly global  
world. As per Public Enterprise Survey Report 2023-24, Research and Development Expenditure of 
79 CPSEs out of 272 operating CPSEs stood at ₹10,813 crore in FY 2023-24 against ₹7,233 crore in 
FY 2022- 23 showing an increase of 49.50 per cent. 
 
The Chapter has covered expenditure on Research and Development activities by 26 selected Ratna 
category CPSEs (Annexure XX) during the period 2019-20 to 2023-24. Audit had applied stratified 
random sampling for selecting the sample of 26 CPSEs out of 100 Ratna CPSEs41 (14 Maharatna, 24 
Navratna, 51 Miniratna (category 1) and 11 Miniratna (category 2) CPSEs) based on their total 
Research and Development expenditure valuing ₹8,165 crore for the year ended 31 March 2023. Of 
these 26 CPSEs, 14 incurred expenditures of more than ₹100 crore, five CPSEs incurred expenditure 
ranging between ₹20 crore and ₹100 crore, four CPSEs incurred expenditure ranging upto ₹20 crore 
and three CPSEs incurred nil expenditure (although their Profit Before Tax was more than ₹100 crore) 
on Research and Development activities during any of the years during 2019-20 to 2023-24. The para 
was issued to 26 CPSEs during July-August 2025 and to the respective Ministries (September 2025). 
The replies received from the Management and the Ministries till 14.01.2026 have been incorporated

4.2 Scope of Audit 

 
 
 
101 
in the chapter. The reply from Ministry of Defence in respect of Hindustan Aeronautics Limited was 
awaited (14 January 2026). 
The objective of audit was to assess whether: 
 CPSEs have Research and Development policy/manual and a roadmap for future plan;  
 Effective procedures and methodologies are in place for monitoring, implementation and 
evaluation of final results from the Research and Development projects; 
 Funds were being expended on Research and Development, as required by the MoU requirement 
of DPE; 
Research and Development expenditure resulted in commercialization of products/ services and has 
ultimately led to benefit to the Company on the ground. 
An Audit chapter on ‘Expenditure on Research and Development by CPSEs’ was included in CAG’s 
Report No. 18 of 2019 based on the DPE’s guidelines (September 2011). However, soon after the 
issue of audit report the guideline was withdrawn (July 2019). No dedicated guidelines are currently 
in place for monitoring the expenditure on Research and Development by CPSEs. Expenditure on 
Research and Development/ innovations, initiatives have been stipulated as one of the performance 
parameters (two marks out  of 100) under the Consolidated MoU Guidelines (March 2022) without 
specific emphasis on performance viz. the patents generated, material costs saved, technology 
developed and commercialised etc. 
 
The audit was carried out based on following criteria: 
 Policy and Plans approved by the Board of Directors and the Vision plan/roadmap of the 
administrative Ministry. 
 Research and Development performance parameter included under MoU guidelines issued by 
DPE. 
 Agenda and Minutes of Meetings of the Boards of Companies. 
 Income Tax benefit applicable under Section 35 of the Income Tax Act related to Research and 
Development expenses. 
 
4.5.1 Policy and planning for undertaking Research and Development activities  
Clear cut structured policy and laid down procedures are needed to guide and steer the Research and 
Development policy activities by CPSEs. The policy should align with the company's overall vision 
and mission, and the plan should detail specific projects, timelines, budgets, and expected outcomes.

policy would be formulated, incorporating periodic monitoring of R&D activities by the Apex 
group. The proposed policy had been submitted to the Board of Directors for approval. 
 Oil India Limited: Research & Development Department was established (1985) and Research 
and Development policy was formulated (2012-2013), which was however not effectuated after 
withdrawal of DPE guidelines on Research and Development activities (June 2019).   
 Coal India Limited (CIL) and Bharat Coking Coal Limited (BCCL):  The Companies 
follow the guideline for Science and Technology Projects. CIL constituted committee (January 
2025) and prepared draft Research and Development polic y document. BCCL formed a 
Research & Development Committee headed by its CMD. Ministry of Coal stated (October 
2025) that as BCCL was a subsidiary, no separate R&D policy was required.

Business Model with limited product innovation and was not having any Research and 
Development policy. 
In the absence of any Government guidelines, the CPSEs were not bound to frame dedicated and 
uniform policy for taking up Research and Development activities to steer its activities to align with 
the Central Government’s ‘Atmanirbhar Bharat” initiative.

by CPSEs needs to be enhanced to meet the minimum parameter stipulated in MoU guidelines.

4.5.3 Implementation mechanism of Research and Development projects 
Successful implementation of Research and Development projects can be ensured by CPSEs by 
establishing structured mechanism for implementation at the beginning of the Research and 
Development projects. Audit noted that majority of the Ratna CPSEs had well defined mechanism in 
place for implementation of Research and Development projects as discussed below45: 
(i) SAIL: RDCIS at Ranchi (the Corporate Research and Development unit of SAIL) 
undertakes Research and Development projects in diverse realms of Iron &  Steel 
Technology under the categories of Plant Performance Improvement, Product Development, 
Scientific Investigation and Development, Basic Research and Technical Services.  
(ii) Airport Authority of India Limited: Airport Authority of India  has an Apex Committee 
for Project Monitoring/Review to monitor the progress periodically and assess the outcomes 
of the projects. AAI has empowered the Apex Committee for Project Monitoring/Review to 
terminate the Project. 
(iii) Coal India Limited: Research and Development activities of Coal India Limited is headed 
by Research and Development Board led by Chairman of the company. To ensure efficient 
decision making, an Apex Committee operates under the Research and Development Board. 
The Central Mine Planning and Design Institute Limited (CMPDI), CIL’s consultancy arm, 
serves as the nodal agency for coordinating and implementing Research and Development 
initiatives. Ministry of Coal stated (October 2025) that all projects undertaken at BCCL are 
funded either by Coal India Ltd. Research & Development grant or Ministry of Coal Science 
& Technology grant with BCCL acting as sub-implementing agency. 
(iv) NALCO: In case of NALCO, National Aluminium Company Limited Research & 
Technology Centre (NRTC) is assisted by local board of advisor s (Research Advisory 
Committee) in planning, implementing, periodical review of Research and Development 
projects and getting necessary approval of the Board.  
(v) NTPC: Research and Development activities in NTPC were guided and steered by the 
Research Advisory Council (RAC) comprising of eminent scientists and experts from India 
and abroad. RAC works under NTPC Energy Technology Research Alliance (NETRA). 
NETRA setup in 2009 as a Research and Development wing of NTPC.    
(vi) HAL: Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) broadly undertook two categories of Research 
and Development projects viz., Customer funded and HAL funded projects. The customer 
funded projects were executed against sanctions approved by the Cabinet Committee on 
Security based on the requirements of the Defence forces. The Design & Development 
projects initiated by HAL were undertaken to build indigenous capability through internal 
resources and corpus created by HAL for in -house Research and Development. HAL 
contributes 10 per cent of the operational Profit after tax annually to this corpus.  
                                                           
45 Excluding BCCL which was a supplementing agency of CIL, and IREDA, TCIL and NSIC wherein no R&D work 
was done.  

 
 
 
108 
(vii) MECON: The Company follows the mechanism of a Standard Operating Procedure and 
Quality manual for taking up any R&D projects. 
(viii) BHEL: The Company has established 14 Centres of Excellence and also carries out R&D 
activities in the Corporate R&D Division, Hyderabad, and the Research and Product 
Development (RPD) centers at its manufacturing units. 
(ix) GAIL: GAIL has been pursuing the R&D activities in a limited manner in areas of business 
/ operation of the company viz. N atural Gas transmission and distribution, Petrochemicals, 
City Gas Distribution, Renewable Energy, Oil and Gas exploration. 
(x) HPCL: HPCL has set up (2016) 'HP Green R&D Centre' at Bengaluru to develop innovative 
& path breaking technologies and products. The  R&D centre is recognized by the 
Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) and has collaborations with 
research institutes in India and abroad. 
(xi) Indian Oil Corporation Limited:  The Company set up (1972) its R&D Centre at 
Faridabad, Haryana. After establishing its brand of lubricants and building the competence 
of supply of lubricants in diverse field of applications, Indian Oil focussed on technologies 
and catalyst in the area of petroleum refining.  
(xii) ONGC: To improve the exploration and production of hydrocarbons and alternative energy 
sources, ONGC signed (2015) a Memorandum of Collaboration (MoC) with seven IITs.  
(xiii) Oil India Limited (OIL): OIL established two knowledge-based R&D Centres - Research 
& Development Department (R&D) at its Field Headquarters in Duliajan, Assam, India and 
Centre of Excellence for Energy Studies (CoEES) in Guwahati, Assam, India.  
(xiv) BEL: It has a Multi-Tier R&D structure and all the R&D centres of BEL are registered with 
Department of Scientific & Indu strial Research (DSIR) and function at various locations 
across India. BEL’s Software Technology Centre at Bangalore, Hyderabad Unit and CRL -
Ghaziabad have been certified to Capability Maturity Model Integration (CMMI) Level 5 
Rating. 
(xv) NMDC: NMDC’s R&D Cent re located at Hyderabad extends technology support to 
NMDC’s in-house projects and other organizations in India. 
(xvi) MDNL: MDNL's R & D takes place against trial order or development order and the heats 
taken for new grades/products are considered for R &D exp enditure. After successful 
completion of Trial order, production orders are placed by customer on MDNL. 
(xvii) ONGC Videsh Limited (OVL):  OVL being a wholly owned subsidiary of ONGC, the 
Company follows ONGC’s established R&D procedures. 
(xviii) BDL: The Company was cont inuously engaged in new product development and up -
gradation of existing products to meet customer requirements. BDL’s Design & Engineering 
division works on development of various projects. 

 
 
 
109 
(xix) BEML: R&D division of BEML provided the company with a technological base for growth 
and coupled with indigenisation, had been key to BEML’s business. Research and 
development in all the three major business verticals of Mining & Construction, Defence & 
Aerospace, and Rail & Metro were carried out at the various complex es dedicated for their 
design development, engineering, manufacturing and testing. 
(xx) CWC: The Research & Development Division carries out studies for improvement in the 
existing methods/systems and exploring new areas to increase efficiency and productivity in 
the field of storage of food grain and notified commodities in order to provide best services 
to customers. 
(xxi) ALIMCO: To foster the R&D of the Corporation, MoU had been entered with leading 
Research apex bodies like ISRO, DRDO, CSIR, IIT -M. The Corporatio n had established 
High-end Prosthesis Shop at ALIMCO Hqrs., Kanpur wherein High Precision Machines 
(including CNCs) had been installed and commissioned. 
(xxii) MDSL: MDSL had undertaken focused R& D initiatives through collaboration with 
academic institutions, start-ups & MSMEs not only in the core defence sector but also other 
critical areas like underwater autonomous technology, sustainable & environment friendly 
transport solutions etc.

4.5.5 Availing of tax benefits by CPSEs on the Research and Development expenditure 
The Specific exemptions available under Section 35 of IT Act/5(2) of IT Rules are as under: 
i. 100 per cent  deduction of revenue expenditure on Scientific Research related to business 
(Section 35(1)(i) of IT Act). 
ii. 100 per cent deduction of capital expenditure on Scientific Research related to business in the 
year the expenditure is incurred; (Section 35(1) (iv) of IT Act). 
iii. Deduction @150 per cent (to the sponsor) for payments made to approved national laboratories, 
universities and IITs or a specified person, with a specific direction that the said sum shall be 
used for scientific research under a programme. (Section 35(2AA) of the IT Act). 
iv. Accelerated depreciation allowance for investment on plant and machinery, made on the basis 
of indigenous technology (Rule 5(2) (a) (b) of IT Rules, 1962).

(B) Customs duty is exempted for in-house Research and Development units established by corporate 
companies, other than a Hos pital for capital equipment and consumables needed for Research and

make discoveries that can help develop new products or way of doing things or work towards 
enhancing pre-existing products or processes.

(80.53 per cent) and earned a total revenue of ₹33,977.35 crore throug h commercialisation of such 
activities. The remaining 10 CPSEs had spent ₹6,655.1 crore (19.47 per cent ) on Research and 
Development activities but were unable to generate revenue through commercialisation. 
In the absence of any Governme nt guidelines, the CPSEs were not bound to frame dedicated and 
uniform policy for taking up Research and Development activities to align with the Central 
Government’s vision of “Atmanirbhar Bharat”. Out of 26 CPSEs selected for audit, more than half 
of them did not have dedicated policy and instead followed Quality policy/ Action plans/ other related 
guidelines/ framework documents etc. The lack of committed focus in the area led to various gaps 
with respect to the expenditure being incurred on Research and Development by the selected CPSEs.  
During 2021-22 to 2023-24, 9-13 CPSEs (Maharatna, Navratna and Miniratna) incurred less than 2 
per cent of Profit Before Tax on Research and Development, whereas, three CPSEs (one Navratna 
and two Miniratna) did not inc ur any Research and Development expenditure during this period. 
Although majority of the selected Ratna CPSEs had well defined mechanism in place for 
implementation of Research and Development projects, there was lack of effective monitoring of 
Research and Development projects. Out of 26 CPSEs only 13 had Apex/Review/Sub-committee for 
periodic monitoring of Research and Development activities. Consequently, there were substantial 
delays ranging between 1 -69 months in completion of Research and D evelopment projects. Out of 
6,783 projects taken up by 22 CPSEs during 2019 -20 to 2023 -24, 5,816 projects were completed, 
including 1,652 projects completed beyond scheduled completion date and 172 that were ongoing but 
delayed.  
The impact of the Research and Development expenditure of ₹34,178.99 crore incurred by 23 CPSEs out 
the 26 selected CPSEs could be seen in the revenue generated through commercialisation by eleven 
CPSEs being ₹33,977.35 crore. 1,670 research papers were got published by 16 CPSEs an d 10 CPSEs 
had not published any research papers. Further, out of 2,436 patents filed for registration by 17 CPSEs, 
952 patents were granted 1,466 patent applications were under process while 18 were rejected.   
The Research and Development activities by Central Public Sector Enterprises are key to the 
strengthening of the nation’s technological capabilities and the expenditure on such activities needs 
to be prioritized to ensure growth, creation of jobs and to enable CPSEs to cope with the challenges 
and opportunities globally. 
 
Recommendation: 
Government may consider developing dedicated policy/guidelines on Research and 
Development activities for CPSEs. 
Mechanisms should be put in place to ensure better monitoring, execution and evaluation of 
Research and Development projects to ensure timely completion and to achieve the envisaged 
impact.  
CPSEs should be encouraged to recognize the strategic importance of R&D through regular 
workshops, webinars, and incentives to drive innovation, improve competitiveness, and 
contribute to long-term business success.

CHAPTER V 
Corporate Social Responsibility 

 
 
 
124 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
125 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) is the continuing commitment by business to behave ethically 
and contribute to economic development while improving the quality of life of the local community 
at large. It recognizes the interests of its stakeholders and the general community at large by covering 
sustainability, social impact and ethics. The concept of CSR rests on the ideology of give and take. 
Companies take resources in the form of raw materials, human resources etc. from society. By 
performing the task of CSR activities, the companies are giving something back to society. 
Legal Framework: CSR funding has been made mandatory in India through provisions of Section 
135 of the Companies Act 2013 . It stipulates that every company having a net worth of rupees five 
hundred crore or more, or turnover of rupees one thousand  crore or more, or a net profit of rupees 
five crore or more during the immediately preceding financial year shall qualify for undertaking CSR 
activities. The Act makes it mandatory for any such company to spend annually at least two per cent 
of average net profit (calculated as per section 198 of the Act) of three immediately preceding 
financial years towards CSR activities. The activities which may be included by Companies in their 
CSR policies are listed in Schedule VII of the Companies Act, 2013. The compliance of the provisions 
of CSR under the Act i.e., constitution of CSR Committee, formulation of CSR Policy and spending 
of prescribed amount on CSR activities came into force from April 2014.  
In February 2014, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) issued Companies (Corporate Social 
Responsibility Policy) Rules, 2014 (amended in January 2021). The CSR Policy Rules were made 
applicable to all companies including CPSEs w .e.f. 1 April 2014. The Department of Public 
Enterprises (DPE) also issued notification on observance of transparency and due diligence in 
selection and implementation of activities under CSR by CPSEs in August 2016. In December 2018, 
DPE issued guidelines  related to utilisation of CSR funds in a focused manner towards national 
priorities by adopting a theme-based approach every year. 
 
Audit had selected 59 CPSEs out of 212 CPSEs under the administrative control of various 
Ministries/Departments which had e arned net profit in FY 2022 -23 (as per data published in the 
Survey Report of DPE) as summarized in the table below. The details of all the profit making CPSEs 
during FY 2022-23 as published in the Survey Report including the list of sampled CPSEs selected  
for detailed audit are given in Annexure XXIA and XXIB.

5.3.1.  Constitution of CSR committee 
As per Section 135 (1) of the Companies Act, 2013 every company meeting the criteria in section 
135 of the Act shall constitute a Corporate Social Responsibility Committee of the Board consisting 
of three or more Directors, out of which at least one Director shall be an Independent Director. 
Further, according to Rule 5(1)(i) of CSR Rules 2014, an unlisted public company covered under 
Section 135(1) is not required to appoint an Independent Director pursuant to Section 149(4) of the 
Act and shall have its CSR Committee without such Director.  
Audit observed that 53 CPSEs out of 58 CPSEs selected for Audit fo rmed a CSR committee as 
required under the Act. Five50 CPSEs did not constitute CSR committee. 
National Film Development Corporation Limited (NFDCL) and Sagarmala Development Company 
Limited (SDCL) were not required to constitute a CSR Committee as the amount to be spent by the 
company under sub-section (5) did not exceed ₹50 lakh as per Section 135 (9) of the Companies Act, 
2013 during 2023-24. Further, three CPSEs, Jammu & Kashmir Developme nt Finance Corporation 
Limited (JKDFCL), North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation Limited

5.3.2 Formulation and approval of CSR policy by the CPSEs 
Section 135(3) of the Act requires that the CSR committee formulate and recommend a CSR policy 
for the company to the Board which shall, as per Section 135(4) approve the same after considering 
the recommendations of the committee.  
Audit observed that 50 out of the 58 CPSEs had framed the CSR policy, which was approved by their 
respective Boards (Annexure XXII). 
In respect of five unlisted CPSEs —National Film Development Corporation Limited, Sagarmala 
Development Company Limited, Central Registry of Securitisation Asset Reconstruction and 
Security Interest of India, MMTC  Limited and Sutlej Jal Vidyut Nigam Limited —the Board itself 
formulated and approved the CSR policy. Two unlisted CPSEs, namely Indian Optel Limited and 
North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation, had not framed a CSR policy. In the 
case of one unlisted CPSE, Instrumentation Limited, the CSR Committee had recommended a policy; 
however, the same was not approved by the Board of Directors.  
DPE in its reply (November 2025) has no comments to offer on the observation. 
5.3.3 Annual CSR Plan and Budget 
As per Rule 5(2) of the amended CSR Rules 2021, the CSR Committee shall formulate and 
recommend to the Board an Annual Action Plan which shall include the list, manner of execution and 
modalities of utilisation of funds for CSR activities and programs that are approved to be undertaken 
in areas specified in schedule VII and may alter such plan at any time during the year on the 
recommendation of the CSR Committee. 
Out of 58 CPSEs, 40 had prepared a CSR Annual Action Plan for FY 2023-24, while 18 CPSEs had 
not formulated such a plan. Audit observed the following in respect of these CPSEs:  

 
 
 
128 
 The CSR Annual Action Plan was not applicable to eight 51 CPSEs. Clarification for non - 
applicability are as follows: 
In case of BCPL obligation for the year 2023 -24 was ₹18.77 lakhs and the same was transferred to 
clean ganga and swacch bharat kosh. NMDFC has the obligation of ₹132 lakh for the FY 2023 -24. 
However, CPSE did not expense the amount and entire amount of ₹13 2 lakh was transferred to 
unspent account. In case of CERSAI current year obligation of ₹179 lakh was set off with ₹255 lakh 
(Excess CSR expenditure incurred in previous years) which was required to be set off in 2023 -24. 
Hence CPSEs namely BCPL, NMDFC and CERSAI did not prepare the annual action plan for 2023-
24. Further, in case of four CPSEs namely NFDC, BHEL, MMTC and NERAMAC, CSR obligation 
for the year 2023-24 was zero. Hence, all four CPSE did not prepare the annual action plan. Further, 
in case of I REDA, Management stated that CSR annual action plan was not applicable as Board 
approved CSR policy of IREDA existing thereon in FY 2023-24 covered earmarking of CSR budget 
under various activities of Schedule VII of Companies Act. 
 Ten52 CPSEs had not formulated a CSR Annual Action Plan for FY 2023-24. 
The Annual Action Plan provides the basic framework which ensures compliance with the applicable 
CSR rules. Thus, it was found that ten companies did not comply with Rule 5 of Companies 
(Corporate Social Responsibility Policy) Amendment Rules, 2021 in planning of the CSR activities 
for 2023-24. 
DPE in its reply (November 2025) has no comments to offer on the observation. 
 
CSR landscape has undergone profound changes, largely catalyzed by enforcing the CSR Rules 2014. 
This directive, mandates companies to allocate two per cent  of their average net profit of three 
preceding financial years towards social development and this mandate has driven a substantial surge 
in resources directed towards development initiatives. As a result, there has been a notable expansion 
in the scope and impact of CSR activities with a growing emphasis on addressing societal challenges 
aligned with n ational goals. Audit observations in this regard are discussed in the succeeding 
paragraphs.

5.4.4 Unspent Amount transferred to Unspent CSR Account  
According to section 135(6), of the Companies Act, 2013, any amount remaining unspent under sub-
section (5), pursuant to any ongoing project, fulfilling such conditions as may be prescribed, 
undertaken by a company in pursuance of its Corporate Social Responsibility Policy, sh all be 
transferred by the company within a period of 30 days from the end of the financial year to a special 
account to be opened by the company in that behalf for that financial year in any scheduled bank to 
be called the Unspent Corporate Social Responsi bility Account. As per section 135(5) unless the 
unspent amount relates to any ongoing project referred to in sub -section (6), such unspent amount 
needs to be transferred to a Fund specified in Schedule VII, within a period of six months of the 
expiry of the financial year. In this regard, audit observed the following. 
i) Out of 58 CPSEs, 18 CPSEs58 were having unspent amount of ₹517.48 crore at the end of 
financial year 2023-24. These 18 CPSEs transferred the remaining unspent CSR budget to 
either Unspent CSR Account or to a fund specified under Schedule VII as per section 135(5) 
of the Companies Act, 2013 within the prescribed time.  
ii) Out of these 18 CPSEs, four CPSEs59 transferred the unspent amount to both Unspent CSR 
Account and to specified fund under Schedule VII. (Annexure XXVII) 
As per rule 4 (5) of Companies (Corporate Social Responsibility Policy) Amendment Rules, 2021, 
“The Board of a company shall satisfy itself that the funds so disbursed have been utilised for the 
purposes and in the manner as approved by it and the Chief Financial Officer or the person responsible 
for financial management shall certify to the effect.” 
                                                           
58 National Minorities Development & Finance Corporation, Electronics Corporation of India Ltd, Hindustan Copper 
Ltd, Shipping Corporation of India Ltd, Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Ltd, Indian Railway Catering 
and Tourism Corporation Ltd, India Infrastr ucture Finance Co. Ltd, Container Corporation of India Ltd, Security 
Printing & Minting Corporation India Ltd, Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd, Steel Authority of India Ltd, Export 
Credit Guarantee Corporation Ltd, Mangalore Refinery & Petrochemicals Limi ted, Bharat Electronics Ltd, Indian

Audit, however, observed in case of Jammu & Kashmir Financial Development Corporation Limited 
(JKFDCL) CFO certification for utilisation of funds disbursed for CSR activities to satisfy the Board 
that the funds of CSR have been utilised for the purposes was not placed at Board meeting while 
placing annual report on CSR for Board’s approval. This resulted in non -compliance to above 
mentioned Rules. 
JKFDCL in reply acknowledged the observation and stated (June 2025) that the presentation of the 
CFO certification, which was meant for Board’s approval, was inadvertently missed and assured 
immediate compliance. 
Further, in case of Instrumentation Limited, Audit observed that a sum of ₹22.47 lakh was earmarked 
to be expended on CSR activities during the year 2023 -24, out of which the management incurred 
₹9.45 lakh on CSR ac tivities. The remaining amount ₹13.02 lakh was deposited in the bank in the 
form of Fixed Deposit by the management.  
Instrumentation Limited stated that suitable projects were not found, resulting in less expenditure. 
However, Company did not open the ded icated account for unspent CSR fund as per section  135 of 
the Companies Act 2013. Thus, the Company did not adhere to the provisions of section 135(5) and 
135(6) of the Companies Act 2013, in respect of disclosure of Unspent amount. 
Instrumentation Limited  stated that the company's primary goal was to ensure CSR funds were 
dedicated solely to CSR purposes. Bank statements confirm the funds were held in fixed deposits 
until utilised, and audited balance sheet disclosures (Note No. 32.6) support this. Additio nally, 
accrued interest will also be used for CSR purposes, aligning with the legislative intent and 
demonstrating responsible fund management. The management further stated (June 2025) that the 
company has requested the bank for creation of lien on Fixed Deposits citing that the same will be 
used only for CSR purpose. Once lien is created, the FD will be released by bank only on satisfaction 
of lien purpose certified by company. 
Management claimed that unspent CSR funds were kept in fixed deposits for future expenditure, with 
proper disclosure in balance sheet.  
However, the Companies Act 2013, requires unspent CSR funds to be deposited in a dedicated 
Unspent CSR Account. 
DPE in its reply (November 2025) stated that, there are only two ways prescribed under  the 
Companies Act, 2013 and CSR Rules to deal with unspent CSR amount. First is to deposit the amount 
in Unspent CSR Account if the amount is allotted to any CSR project, within 30 days and second is 
to deposit the amount in any of the funds mentioned in Schedule VII within 180 days if the amount 
is not allocated to any CSR project at the end of FY.  
DPE reply is silent on the non-compliance to section 135 (5) and (6), of the Companies Act, 2013 by 
the above mentioned CPSEs.

5.4.5 Administrative overheads 
As per Rule 7(1) of CSR Rules 2021, administrative overhead expenditure should not exceed five per 
cent of overall CSR expenditure of the company for the financial year. From 2020 -21 onwards 
additional five per cent expenses of total CSR expenditure for that FY or ₹50 lakh whichever is lower 
were allowed towards impact assessment studies. Audit observed that 29 CPSEs 60 incurred ₹112.03 
crore towards administrative overhead and 20 CPSEs 61 incurred ₹7.47 crore on Impact Assessment 
during 2023 -24 (Annexure XXVIII). Further, 17 CPSEs had incurred expenditure both on 
Administrative overhead as well as on Impact Assessment.  
Audit noticed, excess expenditure on Kits and Administrative Overheads by NTPC. As per the terms 
of the addendum agreement, ₹25 lakh per y ear (total ₹75 lakh over three years) was to be allocated 
for providing kits to Indian archery teams for international competitions. However, Audit observed 
that ₹129.02 lakh has been disbursed towards kits, resulting in an excess expenditure of ₹54.02 lak h 
beyond the approved ceiling. Additionally, an amount of ₹123.80 lakh was paid towards 
administrative expenses claimed by Archery Association of India (AAI) which was over and above 
the costs of organising National Ranking Archery Tournaments (NRATs) and National Archery 
Championship (NACs).  
The Management replied (July 2025) that it was found that ₹30.14 lakh incurred during the financial 
years 2018 -19 and 2020 -21 was inadvertently categorised as kit expenditure, whereas it actually 
related to administrative costs. AAI has acknowledged the error and has committed to rectifying it in 
the forthcoming UCs. The actual expenditure on kitting amounts to ₹99.86 lakh. 
DPE in reply (November 2025) accepted that Administrative overhead need to be calculated from the 
expenditure undertaken by grant maker and no amount from the approved projects to be included in 
this calculation.

5.5.2 Manner of implementation of CSR activities 
Rule 4 of Companies (CSR) Rules 2014 exclusively deals with the way the CSR activity is to be 
undertaken under Section 135 of the Act. The Board may decide to undertake its CSR activities as 
recommended by the CSR committee through a registered trust/ society or companies under Section 
8 of the Act or otherwise. 
As per the information available for 58 CPSEs, the manner of implementation of 1806 projects was 
directly/in-house and 4,063 projects were executed through Government/external agencies, NGOs, 
Society (Annexure XXXI)  
 Four CPSEs undertook in-house projects; (Annexure XXXI A) 
 Six CPSEs outsourced CSR projects to external agencies; (Annexure XXXIB) 
 Thirty-two CPSEs have undertaken both in-house projects as well as outsourced CSR projects 
to external agencies (Annexure XXXIC) and 
 Nine CPSEs did not undertake any projects (Annexure XXXID) 
 Out of remaining seven CPSEs, criteria was not applicable to six CPSEs and for SAIL it was 
as per company’s policy (Annexure XXXIE). 
Out of 4,124 projects implemented through external agencies, CPSEs had resorted to tendering in 
respect of 944 projects; 2,361 projects on a nomination basis and 806 projects were undertaken either 
through Government agencies/institutions, local bodies/community-based organisations or based on 
proposals received from NGOs/implementing agencies etc. Further, audit observed that five70 CPSEs 
have furnished different numbers of total projects/activities carried out by external agencies (4063) 
and break up provided of the same (4124). Hence, 61 projects /activities of five CPSEs remains 
unreconciled. 
Total 55 CPSEs awarded 2,361 projects on a Nomination basis which is not a prudent practice as 
awarding contracts on a nomination basis  should only occur in exceptional and unavoidable 
circumstances, such as during emergencies, when procurement is possible from only a single source, 
or when a supplier has exclusive rights, as detailed in  Central Vigilance Commission  (CVC) 
guidelines. This method is considered a restrictive practice that eliminates competition.

5.5.4 Local areas 
Section 135(5) of the Act provides that the CPSEs shall give preference to the local area and areas 
around it where it operates, for spending the amount earmarked for CSR activities. As per the 
information available in respect of 58 CPSEs, 41 CPSEs defined local area in their CSR policy, 13 
CPSEs72 did not define local area in their CSR policy and for four CPSEs it was not applicable since 
they were not required to spend.   
Further, 40 CPSEs gave preference to local areas, eight CPSEs did not give preference to local area 
and for 10 CPSEs giving preference was not applicable (Annexure XXXIII). 
 
As per Rule 5(2) of CSR Rules 2014, the CSR committee shall institute a transparent monitoring 
mechanism for implementation of CSR projects/programs/ activities undertaken by the CPSE. DPE 
vide OM dated 1 August 2016 instructed the CPSEs to have an institutionalized mechanism for 
monitoring, reporting and evaluation of CSR.

reasons for unspent amount. 
ii. Provide details of the capital asset(s), created or acqu ired (including complete address and 
location of the capital asset).

5.7.3 Asset Creation 
Out of 58 CPSEs, 18 CPSEs (Annexure XXXVI) had created/acquired capital assets, during the year

5.7.4 CSR activities undertaken in pursuance of normal course of business 
In terms of Para 6 of MCA CSR Rules 2014 ‘CSR activities do not include the activities undertaken 
in pursuance of normal course of business of a company’. Para (viii) of the said CSR Rule, June 2014 
also stated that contribution to corpus of a Trust/Society/Section 8 Compani es etc. will qualify as 
CSR expenditure as long as (a) the Trust/Society/Section 8 Companies etc. is created exclusively for 
undertaking CSR activities or (b) where the corpus is created exclusively for a purpose directly 
relatable to a subject covered in Schedule VII of the Act. 
In January 2019, IOCL along with other Oil PSUs signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) 
with Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Bombay to create a Centre of Excellence in Oil, Gas and 
Energy (CEOGE), to provide a competitive advantage to India’s oil and gas industry. As such, an 
expenditure amounting to ₹6.35 crore incurred by the Company during 2023 -24 towards setting up 
and operation of CEOGE was not an eligible CSR activity. 
IOCL replied (May 2025) that centre was set up to work on issues of national importance, to support 
the cause of sustainable development and to bridge knowledge gap in the system through a healthy 
interaction of industry with academia thereby benefitting society as a whole and supporting the cause 
of edu cation through capability building in oil & gas sector. Further, the areas that have been 
identified by CEOGE to work upon are aligned primarily to the causes of enhancing education and 
skills on sustainable development, self - sufficiency through import s ubstitution and environment 
                                                           
74 Bengal Chemicals & Pharmaceuticals Ltd. , Sagarmala Development Company Ltd. , Indian Medicines & 
Pharmaceutical Corporation Ltd. , India Optel Ltd. , Bharat Electronics Ltd. , Northern Coalfields Ltd. , 
Instrumentation Ltd.    

 
 
 
141 
protection as biomass, gas hydrate production, renewable energy, hydrogen as energy vector, energy 
management and low carbon future etc. 
Reply of the IOCL may be viewed in the context that as per the MoU signed between OMCs and 
Bombay CEOGE, the project was intended to provide competitive advantage to the oil and gas sector. 
Since CEOGE is industry-specific and its activities serve business/commercial interests of the sector 
rather than society at large, projecting this as a CSR activity was not in line with the provisions of 
CSR Rules 2014. 
DPE (November 2025) in its response agreed with the observation mentioned. 
5.7.5 Impact Assessment 
As per Rule 8 (3) (a) of the CSR Amended Rules, 2021, every company having average CSR 
obligation of 10 crore rupees or more in pursuance of sub-section (5) of section 135 of the Act, in the 
preceding three financial years shall undertake impact assessment, through an independent agency of 
their CSR projects having outlays of one crore rupees or more and which have been completed not 
less than one year before undertaking impact assessment. Twenty two CPSEs out of 58 CPSEs did 
conduct an impact assessment th rough an independent agency. Eight CPSEs have not conducted 
impact assessment and for remaining 28 CPSEs criteria is not applicable and report ed the same in 
their CSR report (Annexure XXXVII). 
 
Audit observed that in three out of 58 CPSEs, there was a discrepancy in reporting the State wise and 
focus area expenditure. The discrepancy ranged from ₹5.12 lakh to ₹299.10 lakh in the records 
provided to Audit and the corresponding figures disclosed in their financial statements, indicating

5.8 Inconsistencies in Reporting of CSR expenditure 
 

 
 
 
142 
 
At the grassroot level, CSR programs can empower marginalised communities by facilitating access 
to essential provisions and livelihood opportunities. By operating at grassroot levels and targeting 
improving the services that supports the underserved communities, CSR initiatives have the potential 
to effectuate meaningful and sustainable change, thereby significantly contributing to overarching 
development objectives of a country. 
The review of the CSR monitoring framework and implementation practices among CPSEs revealed 
significant discrepancies and areas for improvement. Despite the mandate for a transparent 
monitoring mechanism as per Rule 5(2) of CSR Rules 2014 and subsequent guidelines from the DPE 
and MCA, there was need to institute effective monitor ing, reporting, and evaluation processes in 
large number of CPSEs. The audit observations highlight issues such as irregularities in the frequency 
of CSR project reviews, deficiencies in obtaining utilisation certificates, and improper reporting of 
CSR expenditures. Moreover, the non-compliance with the prescribed reporting formats, inadequate 
disclosure of CSR activities on company websites, and the lack of adherence to asset creation and 
impact assessment requirements indicate a systemic weakness in the e xecution of CSR obligations. 
These findings underscore the necessity for CPSEs to strengthen their CSR governance frameworks 
to ensure accountability, transparency, and alignment with statutory and regulatory guidelines, 
thereby enhancing the effectiveness and credibility of their CSR initiatives.

CHAPTER VI 
Analysis of Memoranda of Understanding 
between Administrative Ministries and 
Navratna CPSEs

Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) is a mutually negotiated agreement between the Management 
of Central Public Sector Enterprise (CPSEs) and the respective Administrative Ministry/ Department 
for evaluation of the performance of CPSEs. MoU is signed before the start of financial year to fix 
the targets in respect of selected parameters and evaluation of the results to measure the performance 
against the targets after the end of financial year. The system of MoU serves as a mechanism of 
assessing CPSEs' performance as per its audited Financial Statements both for listed and non -listed 
CPSEs. 
All CPSEs (Holding  as well as Subsidiaries) are required to sign MoU; holding Companies sign 
MoUs with their Administrative Ministries/ Departments and the Subsidiary Companies sign MoU 
with their respective holding company. However, the holding CPSE may grant exemption from MoU 
in respect of its subsidiaries. 
 
6.2.1  Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) 
The Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) facilitates the signing of MoU between CPSEs and 
Administrative Ministries/ Departments. DPE, vide its MoU Guidelines, specifies  MoU parameters, 
details of evaluation system, key responsibilities and timelines for signing MoU. It also provides a 
mechanism to evaluate the performance of the management of CPSEs by providing a system of MoU 
target setting as well as evaluation of perf ormance parameters through a digital dashboard. This 
dashboard is used by CPSEs/ Ministries/ Departments for entering data, signing, monitoring and 
evaluating of MoU. 
6.2.2  Inter-Ministerial Committee (IMC) 
Inter-Ministerial Committee (IMC) has been entru sted with the responsibility for finalization of 
CPSE-wise MoU parameters every year based on discussion with the concerned CPSE, Ministry/ 
Department and also representatives from other key agencies being members of IMC. It comprises of 
Secretary (DPE) as  Chairperson, representative of Chief Economic Advisor (Department of 
CHAPTER VI 
Analysis of Memoranda of Understanding between 
Administrative Ministries and Navratna CPSEs 
6.1  Introduction 
 
6.2  Institutional Mechanism for MoU 
 

 
 
 
146 
Economic Affairs), Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Statistics and Programme 
Implementation (MoSPI), National Institution for Transforming India (NITI) Aayog and 
Secretary/representative of Administrative Ministry as special invitee and any other expert co -opted 
on need basis.  
IMC finalises the sectoral template/ CPSE-wise MoU parameters for the purpose of MoU evaluation. 
In order to enable the IMC to determine the benchmarks for various parameters, the CPSE is to upload 
the estimated figures of certain financial and physical attributes on the dashboard by 31 December of 
the financial year, previous to that of the MoU year (referred as base year). These figures are updated 
as per actual results of the base year by the CPSE on the dashboard through DPE’s Public Enterprises 
(PE) Survey portal by 31 October of the MoU year. Similarly, by 31 December of the base year, the 
Administrative Ministry/ Department is required to upload sectoral  vision plan for three years with 
annual milestones on the dashboard for consideration at the time of benchmarking by IMC. 
The purpose of sectoral templates is to select and identify the parameters and weightages relevant to 
the core business activities in  that sector and/ or CPSE. IMC will also set the requisite levels of 
performance against each of the parameters, so decided, as benchmarked targets. 
6.2.3  High Power Committee  
At the apex level of institutional arrangement under MoU system, High Powered Committee (HPC) 
lays policy guidelines, as per recommendations of IMC. HPC comprises of Cabinet Secretary as the 
Chairperson of the Committee and CEO (NITI Aayog), Finance Secretary, Secretary (Expenditure), 
Secretary (Statistics & Programme Implementation ), Chairperson (Public Enterprises Selection 
Board), Chief Economic Advisor (Department of Economic affairs) and Secretary (Public 
Enterprises) as members. HPC approves the common template (MoU parameters). 
6.2.4  Fixation of MoU parameters and targets 
The parameters captured in MoU process aim to reflect the economic performance of CPSEs’ 
profitability/ return on the invested capital as per its audited Books of Accounts. These parameters 
are supposed to evaluate competitiveness/ usefulness of the CPSEs in the given commercial space 
instead of merely evaluating their ‘efforts’ in a given business environment. These parameters strive 
to capture physical as well as financial performance of CPSEs by inter alia covering revenue from 
operations, physical output, return on net worth, asset turnover ratio, earnings per share apart from 
capturing the compliance by the CPSEs to DPE guidelines on CSR, and SEBI (LODR) Regulations 
and Companies Act, 2013 provisions regarding corporate governance, procurement from Micro a nd 
Small Enterprises (MSEs) and timelines of repayments to them. The benchmarked target is 
"Excellent" level. 
MoU parameters are clubbed into groups so that weightages of non -applicable parameter(s), if any, 
for a sector/ CPSE can be redistributed to other parameter(s) of the same group. Besides this, certain 
programmes of the Government such as CSR, procurement from GeM/ MSEs etc. are also included 
for compliance by CPSEs, non -compliance of which results in deduction of full marks i.e., there is 
no partial  deduction. MoU parameters and marking pattern have been mentioned in Annexure-
XXXVIII. 

 
 
 
147

shown as below: 
MoU Score MoU Rating 
Score >= 90 Excellent 
Score>= 70 Very Good 
Score>= 50 Good 
Score>= 33 Fair 
Score<  33 Poor 
 
As per DPE Guidelines, once the CPSEs’ data from their audited financial statements is available on 
the dashboard, the score would be automatically calculated against the benchmarked targets. There 
would be no adjustment in MoU score due to changes in exchange rate, price of raw material or 
finished goods or due to offset for any other reason as these are deemed to be normal business activity 
and audited statement of accounts declared shall prevail. CPSEs are assigned marks proportionately 
for achievement from 50  per cent to 100 per cent of target figure for ea ch parameter (except for 
parameters on reduction of losses/ expenses in respect of loss making CPSEs). However, no marks 
are awarded for the parameters having achievement below 50  per cent  of target (except for the 
parameter on Total Return to Shareholders ). Score on all the parameters are added to arrive at an 
aggregate score.

for regular and effective performance evaluation of CPSEs against MoU targets. Therefore, DPE may 
consider prescribing timeline for finalisation and signing of MoUs.  
6.5.1.2  Finalization of MoU without Sectoral Vision Plan of Ministries 
MoU Guidelines state that the parameters in MoU are further indexed to past performance of the 
CPSE, vision of the Administrative Ministry, sectoral benchmarking and peer comparison, if any. 
Further, these Guidelines also state that the Administrative Ministry/ Department will upload on the 
dashboard, the details of Sectoral Vision Plan for three years with annual milestones by 31 December 
of the base year so that the same can be taken into consideration at the time of benchmarking by IMC. 
Audit observed that the Administrative Ministries in respect of five 77 out of six selected CPSEs did 
not prepare and upload their Sectoral Vision Plan on MoU dashboard for finalisation of MoU targets 
for the years 2022-23 and 2023-24. Thus, MoU in respect of these CPSEs were finalised and signed 
without Sectoral Vision Plan on MoU dashboard which was not in line with MoU Guidelines. In view 
of MoU mechanism prescribing roles and responsibilities of the respective entities involved and 
                                                           
77 NMDC, SCI, NALCO, NLC and EIL 

 
 
 
151 
considering the importance of such Vision Plans, these critical inputs are important for target setting 
process of MoU thereby rendering the MoU evaluation imperfect. 
Ministry of Steel replied (July 2025) that the Vision Plan for NMDC had been prepared by N MDC 
and henceforth, NMDC had been requested to upload the Vision Plan on the MoU dashboard. 
Ministry of Ports, Shipping & Waterways replied  (July 2025) that it already had vision document 
Maritime India Vision (MIV), 2030 and Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision (MAKV) 2047 and two officers 
from the Ministry were on the Board of SCI as Government Nominee Directors to ensure compliance 
with the above vision. 
Ministry of Mines (MoM) stated that NALCO uploaded their Vision Plan along with estimated targets 
and the same was endorsed by the Ministry. The MoU targets, which were as per the capacity of 
NALCO, were also deliberated by the Ministry in the IMC. No separate Vision Plan was upl oaded 
for 2022-23 and 2023 -24. Ministry acknowledged the observation and assured to upload separate 
Vision Plan on the dashboard in the future. 
Ministry of Coal (MoC) replied (August 2025) that the Ministry formulated an Annual Action Plan  
every year which  included the production targets and vision of the Ministry, and the same was 
released in the public domain. In consideration of this Action Plan, MoC recommended MoU 
parameters on the DPE portal, which were then considered by MoC and deliberated in IMC meetings 
with peer comparisons and these were factored into MoU finalization as per DPE Guidelines. 
Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas ( MoP&NG) replied (October 2025) that DPE Guidelines on 
the issue of Sectoral Vision Plan were not mandatory in nature. 
The replies may be seen in light of the fact that as per MoU Guidelines, the Sectoral Vision Plan was 
an essential element to be taken into consideration at the time of benchmarking by IMC.

administrative Ministry takes part in IMC meeting wherein the targets were deliberated upon for 
recommendation to HPC for its approval. Moreover, the representation for revision of parameters/ 
targets should have been made in time. 
6.5.1.4  Signing of MoU by holding CPSE with subsidiary 
As per DPE Guidelines, all CPSEs (holding and subsidiaries) were required to sign MoU. Holding 
companies would sign MoU with their Administrative Ministries and subsidiary CPSEs would sign 
MoU with their respective h olding companies. Further, the holding companies were free to grant 
exemption to its subsidiary companies from signing MoU but the process of exemption would 
ordinarily be completed by 31 March of the base year (i.e., the financial year previous to that of  the 

 
 
 
153 
MoU financial year). As such, the process of exemption from signing of MoU for 2022-23 and 2023-
24 was required to be completed by 31 March 2022 and 31 March 2023 respectively.  
In this regard, Audit observed that: 
A. Delay in signing MoU with subsidiary 
Out of six selected CPSEs, two CPSEs (HAL and NLC) signed the MoU with their subsidiaries within 
time, two CPSEs (NMDC and SCI) had exempted their subsidiaries from signing MoU and one CPSE 
(NALCO) did not have subsidiary. However, in case of one CPSE (EIL), the MoU with its subsidiary 
Certification Engineers International Limited (CEIL) for the year 2023-24 was signed on 2 February 
2024 i.e., in the last quarter and almost at the end of financial year 2023 -24. As such, CEIL was left 
with very little time to achieve the targets.  
EIL replied (July 2025) that the MoU for 2023-24 was signed on 27 September 2023 and e-signed on 
04 October 2023 on consolidated basis with CEIL’s contribution included in the financial parameters. 
After signing of MoU, CEIL was apprised of the same and the preparation of MoU between EIL and 
CEIL was initiated. The preparation and signing of the same got delayed and was signed on  
2 February 2024. However, it was assured that the efforts would be made towards timely signing of 
MoU with the subsidiary in future. 
MoP&NG noted (October 2025) the audit observation. 
B. Delay in granting exemption to subsidiary companies for signing MoU  
Out of six selected CPSEs, in case of two CPSEs viz., SCI and NMDC, there was delay in granting 
exemption to subsidiary from signing MoU for the years 2022 -23 and 2023 -24. SCI granted 
exemption to its subsidiary Inland Coastal Shipping Limited (ICSL) from signing MoU for the year 
2022-23 and 2023-24 on 21 December 2022 and 31 May 2023 respectively i.e., with a delay of nine 
months and two months respectively.  
Further, in case of NMDC, it neither signed MoU with its subsidiary CPSEs (J&K Mineral 
Development Corporation Limited, Karnataka Vijayanagar Steel Limited and NMDC CSR 
Foundation) nor exempted its subsidiaries from signing of MoU for the year 2023-24.  
SCI )June 2025) and MoPSW (July 2025) accepted the audit observation and assured to issue letter 
of exemption to Subsidiaries well within the time limit provided by DPE in future. 
NMDC replied (June 2025) that the Company had taken decision not to enter MoU with its 
subsidiaries as the same were in the stage of ‘awaiting statutory clearances/ allotment of Mines/no 
regular manpower’ and exemption process was not required. 
MoS replied (July 2025) that a s per DPE guidelines, holding company is free to take a decision 
regarding exemption from MoU for its subsidiary companies. 
The reply of NMDC may be viewed in the light of the fact that for the year 2022-23, NMDC requested 
(29 March 2022) the Ministry for exemption of MoUs for subsidiaries and the Ministry informed (13 

 
 
 
154 
May 2022) the DPE that no MoU was proposed to be signed by subsidiary companies with NMDC 
for the year 2022 -23. Similar process of exemption of MoUs for subsidiary companies for the year 
2023-24 was not initiated by NMDC.  
6.5.1.5 Unrealistic target set by DPE for physical production parameter 
In the MoU finalised by DPE for NALCO for the year 2023 -24, as against the physical production 
parameter carrying 20 marks, the targets were set exceeding the Company’s installed and normative 
capacities as discussed below: 
(i)  NALCO’s installed capacity for Aluminium cast metal production was 4.60 lakh tonne per 
annum. However, MoU target for FY 2023 –24 was set by DPE at 5.52 lakh tonne, representing an 
overestimation of approximately 20 per cent. This target exceeded the maximu m achievable output 
based on existing infrastructure, making it operationally unrealistic. 
(ii) The normative capacity for Alumina Hydrate was 21.00 lakh tonne per annum, yet the MoU target 
set by DPE for FY 2023–24 was fixed at 25.93 lakh tonne, exceeding both the normative and installed 
capacities thereby making it evidently unachievable. 
As per performance evaluation report for 2023 -24, the Company could not achieve both the 
production targets as it could achieve 4.63 lakh tonne as against the MoU target  of 5.52 lakh tonne 
for Aluminium cast metal production and 21.24 lakh tonne as against the MoU target of 25.93 lakh 
tonne for Alumina Hydrate production. 
Thus, DPE should have reviewed the target -setting mechanism to ensure alignment with realistic 
operational capabilities. 
NALCO (June 2025) agreed with the audit observation and stated that setting production targets 
beyond its installed capacity made them unrealistic and unachievable. 
Ministry of Mines replied (August 2025) that this was taken up with DPE  to reduce the physical 
targets. Communications were sent to DPE in draft stage but DPE did not consider it.  
DPE replied (September 2025) that there was no downward revision in target for production over the 
years but it was gradually increased to push the CPSE to enhance its capacity. 
The reply may be viewed in light of the fact that while deliberating upon the target for this parameter, 
the IMC, despite noting that the production capacity was in line with historical performance, retained 
the higher target considering the same aspirational in nature. Actual achievement of the production 
parameters also corroborates that realistic target had not been set by DPE despite requests by NALCO 
and the Ministry. 
6.5.1.6  Absence of parameters regarding physical performance  
MoU Guidelines for 2022 -23 and onwards stipulated that in order to measure physical output 
(Production/ Generation/ Transmission/ Value of Production/ Total Income), the CPSEs in 
Petroleum, Power, Mines, Steel, etc. are expected to give information about i nstalled capacity, 

 
 
 
155 
capacity utilization and production as per Annual Report. The parameter can be given in absolute 
quantities or per cent utilization of Capacity or in ₹ crore. 
Audit, however, observed that MoU of NMDC, NALCO, and NLC had only one parameter of 
production/power generation having a weightage of 20 marks; other two parameters viz. installed 
capacity and capacity utilization were not included in MoU. Accordingly, CPSEs could not be 
assessed on the information related to their installed capacity and capacity utilization due to non -
inclusion of these two parameters as per details are given below:

about installed capacity, capacity utilization and production as per Annual Report. Though production 
targets are finalised by IMC based on various factors, the inclusion of parameters regarding installed

6.5.2  Non-deduction of marks despite non-compliance of MoU parameters  
6.5.2.1 Compliance parameter on Companies Act and SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 
As per the MoU Guidelines issued by DPE for the year 2022-23 and onwards, three marks would be 
deducted from the total MoU score achieved by the CPSEs for non -compliance of provisions of the 
Companies Act, 2013 or SEBI (Listing Obligations & Disclosure Requirements) Regulation, 2015 
for listed entities on Corporate Governance. 
Audit observed that despite non -compliance of the provisions of SEBI (LODR) Regulations on 
Corporate Governance, Administrative Ministries and DPE did not deduct three marks from the MoU 
score of the CPSEs as required in MoU Guidelines, as discussed below: 
A. Independent Directors  
The presence of Independent Director on the Board of a Company is important to bring an element 
of objectivity to Board process in order to improve Corporate Governance in the general interest of 
the company and thereby to the benefit of minority interest and smaller shareholders who cannot 
otherwise get their voice heard.  
As per Regulation 17(1)(b) of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 regarding composition of Board of 
Director of listed companies, “where the listed entity does not have a regular non -executive 
chairperson, at least half of the Board of Directors shall comprise of Independent Directors”.  
Audit observed that the Board of Directors of NMDC, SCI, EIL, HAL and NLC were not represented 
by the required number of Independent Directors during the years 2022 -23 and 2023-24 as detailed 
below:
