B. Independent Woman Directors  
As per Regulation 17(1)(a) of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015, regarding composition of Board of 
Directors, “the Board of Directors shall have an optimum combination of executive and non -

 
 
 
157 
executive directors with at least one -woman Director. Further, Board of Directors of the top 1000 
listed entities shall have at least one independent woman director.” 
Audit observed that all the selected CPSEs, except NMDC, were having independent woman Director 
on the Board during 2022-23 and  2023-24.  
As such, there was non-compliance of SEBI provisions regarding independent/ independent woman 
directors but no marks were deducted by DPE for such non-compliance. 
NMDC replied (June 2025) that the Company had claimed marks as the composition of the Board 
was not in the ambit of CPSE. 
Ministry of Steel replied ( July 2025) that the compliance parameter regarding composition of the 
Board of Directors was evaluated in the Ministry. However, since the appointment of Directors is not 
within the ambit of CPSE, this parameter was considered not applicable. 
SCI replied ( September 2025) that it requested multiple times to Ministry of Ports, Shipping and 
Waterways (MoPSW) for appointment of Independent Director on SCI Board mentioning the 
penalties levied by both stock exchanges and other punitive actions which are stated t o be initiated 
by them in the penalty letters. 
MoPSW replied (July 2025 ) that SCI and MoPSW had approached DPE on multiple occasions, 
requesting nominations. MoPSW further stated that the final MoU rating was determined by IMC, 
chaired by the Secretary DPE, representative from SCI, MoPSW and other relevant ministries. All 
MoU parameters are thoroughly deliberated during these meeting before final MoU score is awarded.  
EIL replied (July 2025) that non-compliance is solely on account of non-availability of Independent 
Directors which is beyond the control of EIL, as the appointing authority is the Govt. of India. 
MoP&NG replied (October 2025) that appointment of Independent Director on the Board of CPSEs 
is multi-layered and continuous process. Every endeavour is made by Ministry to ensure that the DPE/ 
SEBI Guidelines are adhered. Due  to such efforts, recently Independent Directors have been 
appointed in EIL in May 2025 with the approval of Appointment Committee of the Cabinet. 
HAL replied (August 2025) that Ministry of Defence has recommended to DPE to waive off the 
Corporate Governance parameter for both the years 2022-23 and 2023-24. The recommendation was 
considered by DPE and marks were not deducted for the compliance parameter relating to Corporate 
Governance in the MoU evaluation of HAL for the years 2022 -23 and 2023-24. However, DPE has 
not issued separate waiver letter in this regard. 
Ministry of Defence (MoD) replied (September 2025) that on the request of HAL, MoD sent letter to 
DPE requesting not to penalize with negative markings in Corporate Governance parameters of the 
MoU for the years 2022 -23 and 2023 -24 and accordingly, marks were not deducted in MoU 
evaluation for the years 2022-23 and 2023-24. 
NLC replied (September 2025) that the matter has been taken up with the Ministry of Coal (MoC) 
for appointment of Independent Directors. 
MoC replied (September 2025) that the Ministry had constituted a Shortlisting Committee to examine 
the empanelment of Independent Director. After shortlisting by the committee, two new Independent 
Directors have been appointed in the Board of NLC in March 2025. 

 
 
 
158 
Replies may be viewed in light of the fact that due to absence of Independent Directors on the Board 
during 2022-23 and 2023-24, CPSEs could not comply with the provisions of Companies Act, 2013 
and SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015. 
Replies of the concerned Administrative Ministries may also be viewed in light of the fact that the 
Ministries could not ensure appointment of Independent Directors and this aspect was not reflected 
in the assessment of performance also. Audit took note of the fact that the Independent Directors have 
been appointed in NLC and EIL in March 2025 and May 2025 respectively i.e., in FY 2025-26. 
6.5.2.2 Exemption from compliance of parameter on Corporate Governance  
As per MoU Guidelines, a group of parameters has been included in the MoU regarding compliance 
of the Companies Act, 2013 {or SEBI (LODR) Regulations in case of listed entities} on Corporate 
Governance. DPE Guidelines stipulate negative marking if these compliance requirements are not 
fulfilled by CPSEs. A to tal of five sub parameters for compliance related to Corporate Governance 
by the CPSEs have been prescribed with a total negative marking of 3 marks (each compliance 
parameter having a weightage of 0.60 marks) for non-compliance. 
In this regard, Audit observed that the Ministry of Defence (MoD) recommended DPE to waive off 
the Corporate Governance parameter for both the years 2022 -23 and 2023-24. The recommendation 
was considered by DPE and marks were not deducted for the compliance parameters relating to 
Corporate Governance in MoU evaluation of HAL for the years 2022 -23 and 2023 -24. However, 
DPE has not issued separate waiver letter in this regard. 
Also, HAL being a listed Company, any such exemption from compliance of rules laid down in this 
regard should have been duly approved by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI). As 
such, DPE should have deducted 3 marks from MoU Score of HAL for the years 2022-23 and 2023-
24. However, HAL secured “Excellent” rating for 2022 -23 and 2023 -24 with a score o f 91.50 and 
92.50 respectively.  
DPE replied (September 2025) that no penalties were imposed as the CPSE was not at fault regarding 
compliance of the corporate governance parameters although no exemptions were granted by DPE 
for the same.  
The reply may be  seen in light of the fact that inclusion of such aspects in MoU as a compliance 
parameter, which are not in control of CPSE, was against the spirit of MoU process to that extent. 
6.5.2.3  Compliance parameter on ‘Health and Safety improvement of Human Resources in 
CPSEs’ 
As per MoU Guidelines, target in respect of compliance parameter ‘Health and Safety improvement 
of Human Resources in CPSEs’ was required to be prescribed by Administrative Ministry and non -
compliance of this compliance parameter would attract deduction of one mark. 
Audit observed that in respect of two CPSEs (EIL and SCI), no specific target for MoU compliance 
parameter ‘Health and Safety improvement of Human Resources in CPSE’ was fixed by the 
concerned Administrative Ministries for 2022-23 and 2023-24 MoU.  However, DPE has mentioned 

 
 
 
159 
compliance with this parameter and did not deduct any mark in the evaluation report of the MoU for 
the years 2022-23 and 2023-24. 
MoP&NG (October 2025) replied that fixing of the HSE targets was a g eneral DPE Guidelines and 
EIL, being consultancy CPSE, followed its HSE policy. 
MoPSW replied (July 2025) that SCI was in compliance with ISO 45001:2018 (Occupational Health 
and Safety Management System  ) onboard all vessels and shore establishments and MoP SW has 
initiated the practice of setting specific targets for the improvement of Health and Safety of Human 
Resources.  
Replies may be viewed in light of the fact that concerned Administrative Ministry did not prescribe 
specific target for Health & Safety improvement of Human Resources as per DPE Guidelines. 
6.5.2.4  Non-inclusion of Compliance Parameter - ‘Target as given by NITI Aayog on Assets 
Monetization Milestone’  
Audit observed that in the signed MoUs between all selected CPSEs with their administrative 
Ministries for the year 2023-24, there was a compliance Parameter “Target as given by NITI Aayog 
on Assets Monetization Milestone”. 
However, it was observed that during evaluation of the performance of these CPSEs with respect to 
their MoU t argets for the year 2023 -24, this compliance parameter was removed from the DPE 
portal/dashboard, though this compliance parameter was part of e-signed MoUs. 
Further, as per DPE guidelines, the target for MoU compliance parameter ‘Assets Monetization 
milestones’ was to be fixed based on the target given by NITI Aayog and verification of achievement 
of this target by the CPSE was to be done by the Administrative Ministry based on confirmation from 
NITI Aayog. However, for the year 2022 -23, this compliance parameter was verified by MoP&NG 
in respect of EIL on the basis of their Board Resolution and confirmation from NITI Aayog was not 
obtained. For non-compliance of this parameter, deduction of one mark was prescribed in the e-signed 
MoU. 
EIL/ MoP&NG replied (July 2025/ October 2025) that the above compliance parameter was part of 
its evaluation report approved by Board and subsequently submitted to DPE. However, system 
generated evaluation report available at DPE’s MoU Portal was not reflecting the same. 
Replies may be viewed in light of the fact that this compliance parameter as mentioned in the signed 
MoUs should had been retained by DPE on the MoU portal at the time of evaluation of performance 
to adjust the non-compliance of the said parameter to reflect th e actual performance achievement of 
CPSEs against the MoU Targets. 
Thus, due to non-retention of the compliance parameters, mentioned in the signed MoU, on the MoU 
Portal at the time of MoU evaluation, the actual performance of CPSEs against the finalized MoU 
targets could not be reflected to that extent. 
DPE reply in this regard was awaited.

6.5.2.5  Impact of CAG’s observations/recommendations on MoU evaluation  
As per MoU Guidelines, while working out the achievement of the year, quantified qualification of 
CAG/ Statutory Auditor would be adjusted in case of overstatement of revenue/profit/surplus or 
understatement of loss/ deficit.  
In respect of NMDC, Audit observed that two comments80 were issued by the C&AG on the Annual 
Accounts of NMDC for the year 2023-24. However, the Company did not consider the effect of the 
C&AG’s comments while furnishing the self -evaluation in terms of EBITDA as a percentage of 
revenue and (ii) Return of capital employed. 
NMDC replied (June 2025) that DPE has adjusted the profit based on C&AG’s comments on financial 
position in 2023 -24 for ₹12.39 crore in compliance with MoU Guidelines 2023 -24 and given final 
marks. 
The reply confirms that the Company did not consider the adjustment of profit during self-evaluation. 
Moreover, the Management did not provide the supporting documents to verify the adjustment made 
by the DPE in profit based on C&AG’s comments. 
MoS did not furnish any comment on this observation.

Audit, however, observed that no timelines were fixed in MoU Guidelines for the final submission of 
scoring/ ranking of MoU to the concerned CPSE by DPE.

Considerable time taken in finalization of the ranking/ scoring of CPSEs was not only against the

DPE replied (September 2025) that the MoU mechanism is not a tool intended for providing feedback 
or facilitating course corrections for CPSEs. The time taken in evaluation does not affect CPSE’s

performance beforehand. MoU evaluation by DPE is confined to verifying and declaring CPSE’s 
MoU ratings.  
DPE reply may be seen in light of the fact that as per MoU Guidelines, the main purpose of MoU 
evaluation is to undertake regular performance evaluation of CPSEs to assess their efficacy towards 
fulfilment of core objectives for which they have been constituted. Hence, the ranking of the CPSEs 
should be done in reasonable time so that other stakeholders are also aware of th e performance of 
CPSEs and corrective measures may be taken by the CPSEs. 
6.5.3.3  Revision/reduction of CAPEX target after e-signing of MoU  
MoU between MoP&NG and EIL for the year 2022 -23 was e-signed on 21 December 2022 i.e., at 
the end of third quarter of 2022-23. In the MoU, CAPEX was one of the parameter and target for this 
parameter was ₹160 crore. After e -signing of MoU, target against CAPEX parameter w as reduced 
(February 2023) from ₹160 crore to ₹70 crore i.e., by 56.25 per cent. DPE also evaluated CAPEX 
parameter on the basis of revised/ reduced MoU target.  
EIL/ MoP&NG replied (July 2025/ October 2025) that the CAPEX was revised at the time of 
preparation of revised estimates to ₹70 crore based on our internal evaluation and the same was put 
up to the Ministry for their approval. The said revision was made part of the Budget Circular and 
Revised CAPEX of ₹70 crore got reflected in the Statement 26 of Budget document of Union 
Government which was published in February 2023 after finalization and signing of MoU for the 
year 2022-23. 

 
 
 
163 
Reply may be viewed in light of the fact that target for CAPEX parameter was revised after e-signing 
of MoU which itself wa s signed at the end of third quarter of 2022 -23. As such, the CPSE had 
sufficient time for internal evaluation and making request to the MoP&NG before signing of MoU.  
6.5.4  Non-hosting of MoU on website of CPSE and administrative Ministry 
While forwarding portal generated MoU to NMDC (23  September 2022) and EIL (09  September 
2022) alongwith their Administrative Ministries, DPE requested to sign the MoU within stipulated 
time period   and post the same on their websites. 
Audit observed that NMDC/ MoS and EIL/ MoP&NG did not host the MoU signed for the years 
2022-23 and 2023-24 respectively. 
NMDC replied (June 2025) that it has posted the MoU in their website (intranet) for information to 
all employees. 
MoS replied (July 2025) that NMDC has been advised to upload the signed copy of MoU on their 
website and the Ministry has also uploaded the MoU for the year 2022 -23 on Ministry’s website. 
Ministry further replied that henceforth, all signed MoU will be uploaded on Ministry’s website. 
EIL (July 2025 ) replied that MoU was published at its intranet which is accessible to all EIL 
employees to disseminate information on the respective targets. 
MoP&NG, while concurring the reply of EIL, stated (October 2025) that hosting of MoU on company 
website is not a mandatory requirement as per DPE guidelines.  
The replies of NMDC and EIL may be viewed in the light of the facts that despite DPE’s directives, 
the MoU were hosted only on the intranet which could be accessed by employees and not hosted on 
the website.

CHAPTER VII 
Disinvestment Process 

 
 
 
166 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
167 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM) under the Ministry of 
Finance deals with all matters relating to the management of investments of Central Government in 
equity including disinvestment of equity in Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs). The major 
areas of its work relate to strategic disinvestment including privatisation and minority stake sale. 
The current disinvestment policy of the Government of India includes disinvestment through minority 
stake sale and strategic disinvestment of CPSEs. In order to redefine public sector participation in 
business enterprises and to encourage private sector participation, the New Public Sector Enterprise 
(PSE) Policy for Atma Nirbhar Bharat was notified on 4 February 2021.The policy intends to 
minimise the presence of Government in PSEs across all sectors of economy and also provides overall 
guidance on strategic disinvestment. The salient features of the policy are as follows: 
 The New PSE policy delineates four81 strategic sectors based on the criteria of national security, 
energy security, critical infrastructure, provision of financial services and availability of 
important minerals. In strategic sectors, the bare minimum presence of the existing public sector 
commercial enterprises at Holding Company level would b e retained under Government 
control. The remaining would be considered for privatisation or merger or subsidiarisation with 
another PSE or for closure.  
 All PSEs in non -strategic sectors shall be considered for privatisation, wherever feasible, 
otherwise such enterprises shall be considered for closure. 
This policy does not apply to certain classes of public sector entities such as Not-for-profit companies, 
or CPSEs providing support to vulnerable groups, or having developmental/promotional roles, etc.  
The Government of India decided (19 April 2022) that PSEs (Central/State/Joint)/ State 
Governments/ Cooperative Societies controlled by the Government (i.e. where 51 per cent or more 
ownership is held by the Central Government/State Government/jointly by Central and/or State 
Governments) are not permitted to participate in the strategic disinvestment/ privatisation  of other 
PSUs as bidders unless otherwise specifically approved by the Central Government in public interest. 
                                                           
81 (i) Atomic Energy, Space and Defence; (ii) Transport and Telecommunications; (iii) Power, Petroleum, 
Coal and other minerals and (iv) Banking, Insurance and Financial Services. 
CHAPTER VII 
Disinvestment Process 
7.1  Disinvestment Policy of the Government of India 

 
 
 
168 
The Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) had issued guidelines (13 December 2021) to 
operationalise the New Public Sector Enterprise policy which inter-alia provides for the identification 
of CPSEs either for closure or privatisation in non-strategic sectors in consultation with the concerned 
Administrative Ministries/Departments, NITI Aayog, Department of Expenditure and DIPAM. 
The Government of India empowered (1 June 2022) the Board of Directors of the PSEs to recommend 
and undertake transactions for disinvestment (both strategic disinvestment and minority stake sale) 
or closure of any of their subsidiaries or units or sale of stake in Joint Ventures. It was also approved 
that based on the proposal of the  Board of the CPSE and the Administrative Ministry, DIPAM will 
obtain an ‘in -principle’ approval of Alternative Mechanism 82. Thereafter, the Board of CPSEs can 
undertake the process of disinvestment or closure of subsidiaries/units/Joint Ventures based on 
DIPAM or DPE guidelines.  
DIPAM issued (14 September 2022) guiding principles for strategic disinvestment/minority stake 
sale of subsidiaries/units/sale of stakes in Joint Ventures by the holding/parent PSEs, whereas DPE 
issued (31 October 2022) guiding principles for closure of subsidiaries/units by their holding/parent 
PSEs. 
 
The Government adopts different modes of disinvestment, which are as under:   
(i) Strategic Disinvestment: It implies entire or substantial sale of Government shareholding of a 
CPSE along with transfer of management control. In case of privatisation, which is a sub -set of 
strategic disinvestments, the Government equity in CPSE and its management control is tra nsferred 
to a private strategic buyer(s) and in other cases of strategic disinvestment, the Government equity is 
transferred to another CPSE along with control.  
(ii) Minority stake sale: In some CPSEs, minority stake sales are carried out without transfer  of 
management control by various methods approved by Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) 
in order to unlock the value, promote public ownership, meet the minimum public shareholding norms 
of SEBI and ensuring higher degree of accountability thro ugh Initial Public Offer (IPO), Further 
Public Offer (FPO), Offer for Sale (OFS), Buyback of shares, Exchange Traded Fund (ETF) etc., as 
explained below:  
 Initial Public Offer (IPO): When an unlisted company makes either a fresh issue of shares or 
convertible securities or offers its existing shares or convertible securities for sale or both for 
the first time to the public, it is called an IPO.  
 Further Public Offer (FPO): When an already listed company makes either a fresh issue of 
shares or convertible securities to the public or an offer for sale to the public, it is called FPO.  
                                                           
82 Alternative Mechanism comprises Minister of Finance, Minister of Road Transport and Highways and Minister of 
Administrative Ministry of the concerned CPSE. 
7.2  Modes of Disinvestment  
 

 
 
 
169 
 Offer For Sale (OFS) is a simpler method of sale of shares through the exchange platform for 
listed companies. The method was largely adopted by listed companies, both state -run and 
private, to adhere to the SEBI norms of minimum public shareholding. Government has often 
used this route to divest its shareholding in CPSEs. 
 Buyback of Shares: It is the repurchase by a company of its shares from the existing 
shareholders that reduces the number of its shares in the open market. 
 Exchange Traded Funds (ETF): Under this method, a basket of CPSE stocks is used as a major 
instrument for disinvestment by the Government. However, due to limited scope of 
disinvestment through existing ETF window, the Government has decided to pause employing 
equity ETFs as a tool for minority stake sale during the year 2023-24. 
 
7.3.1  Strategic Disinvestment of CPSEs: 
(i) CPSEs under Strategic Sectors: 
 NITI Aayog recommends CPSEs to be retained under Government Control or to be considered 
for privatisation or merger or subsidiarisation with another PSE or for closure.  
 NITI Aayog’s recommendations are submitted to the Core Group of Secretaries on 
Disinvestment83 (CGD).  
 CGD’s recommendations are put to the Alternative Mechanism (AM).  
 AM approves the CPSEs to be retained under Government control or to be considered for 
privatisation or merger or subsidiarisation with another PSE or for closure.  
 DIPAM obtains in-principle approval of the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) 
for the strategic disinvestment of the CPSE.  
 DIPAM appoints Transaction Advisors/Legal Advisor/Asset Valuers through tendering, with 
the approval of Inter-Ministerial Group (IMG).  
 Further, a two-stage bidding process (EoI/RFP) is followed. In each stage, the process passes 
through multi-layer decision making mechanism as per the approved process.  
(ii) CPSEs under non-Strategic Sectors:  
 DPE identifies the CPSEs either for closure or privatisation in consultation with the concerned 
Administrative Ministries/Departments, NITI Aayog, Department of Expenditure and DIPAM.  
                                                           
83 Core Group of Secretaries on Disinvestment is headed by Cabinet Secretary and comprise s Secretary (Department of 
Economic Affairs), Secretary (Revenue), Secretary (Expenditure), Secretary (DIPAM), Secretary (Corporate Affairs), 
Secretary (Legal Affairs) and Secretary of the Administrative Department.  
7.3  Process of Disinvestment  

 
 
 
170 
 DPE takes in -principle approval of CCEA regarding the CPSEs identified for closure and/or 
for disinvestment.  
 DPE communicates in-principle approval of CCEA to DIPAM for privatisation/ disinvestment 
of CPSE. However, in case of closure, the process is initiated by the Administrative Ministry. 
 DIPAM takes further actions as per the extant procedure. 
7.3.2  Disinvestment process in case of minority stake sale: 
(i) Minority stake sale through IPO/FPO:  
 In principle consent by the Administrative Ministry of the CPSE concerned is taken. 
 CCEA approves disinvestment of minority stake in the CPSE through IPO/FPO.  
 A High-Level Committee84 (HLC) is constituted to guide and oversee the disinvestment 
process.  
 DIPAM constitutes the Inter -Ministerial Group 85  (IMG). Appointment of Advisors 
(Merchant Bankers/Book Running Lead Managers and Legal Advisers) is done by the 
Inter-Ministerial Group for the proposed transaction.  
 Draft Red Herring Prospectus (DRHP) to be filed with SEBI. 
 High Level Committee after considering the advice of the Book Running Lead Manager 
recommends price band/floor price to Alternative Mechanism (AM). 
 DIPAM, along with the Administrative Ministry and CPSEs, undertakes international and 
domestic Non-deal Roadshows 
 Red Herring Prospectus (RHP) to be filed with SEBI. 
 Alternative Mechanism decides on the price band/floor price, method of disinvestment, 
and price discount for retail investors and employees.  
(ii) Minority stake sale through OFS:  
 DIPAM constitutes the Inter -Ministerial Group (IMG). IMG appoints Merchant Bankers -
cum-Selling Brokers (MBSB) and Legal Advisors (LA) to assist in the process. 
 Merchant Bankers recommend the timing, number of shares and discount to be offered. 
MBSB, along with concerned CPSE, Administrative Ministry  and DIPAM undertake Non-
Deal Roadshows. 
                                                           
84 High Level Committee comprises of Secretary, Joint Secretary and Financial Advisor of DIPAM and Secretary, Joint 
Secretary and Financial Advisor of the concerned Administrative Ministry.  
85 Inter-Ministerial Group comprises of representation from DIPAM, Administrative Ministry, Department of Economic 
Affairs (DEA), Department of Public Enterprises (DPE), Department of Expenditure (DoE) and M/o Legal Affairs.  
 

 
 
 
171 
 Legal Advisors are responsible for preparation of legal documents in line with the existing 
statutory mandates.  
 DIPAM constitutes High Level Committee (HLC) consisting of officers from DIPAM and 
Administrative Ministries/Departments.  
 HLC considers the recommendations of MBSB and makes recommendations to AM on 
quantum, mode and extent of disinvestment, percentage of reservation, discount to the retail 
investors and fixing floor price etc., for further divestment of paid-up equity out of GoI 
shareholding in CPSE. 
 Alternative Mechanism considers HLC's recommendation and gives its approval 
7.3.3 Buyback of Government Shareholding by a CPSE: 
 CPSE’s Board of Directors considers Buyback as per the provisions contained in the 
Companies Act and the existing guidelines issued by DIPAM based on its net worth and 
cash balance, unless exempted by the Inter -Ministerial Committee namely, Committee for 
Monitoring of Capital Management and Dividend in CPSEs (CMCDC). The HLC 
recommends to Alternative Mechanism on the Government's participation in CPSE’s offer 
of buyback.  
 Alternative Mechanism approves the participation of the Government in the Buyback and 
offer of Government’s equity in the Buyback. 
 
The Budget Estimate for receipts through disinvestment for the year 2023 -24 was fixed by the 
Department of Economic Affairs (DEA) at ₹51,000 crore. However, at the Revised Estimates stage, 
“Miscellaneous Capital Receipts - Receipts” were estimated at ₹30,000 crore, which were to account 
for the receipts under erstwhile categories of disinvestment and other capital receipts such as asset 
monetisation. No specific estimates for disinvestment were made in the Revised Estimates for the 
year 2023-24 as well as the Budget Estimates for the year 2024-25. 
The actual disinvestment receipts during the year 2023-24 were ₹16,507.29 crore i.e. 45 per cent less 
than the revised estimate for Miscellaneous Capital Receipts. 
The discontinuation of the target based disinvestment approach was also deliberated by the Standing 
Committee on Finance (Eighteen Lok Sabha) (Demands for Grant 2024 -25). The Committee noted 
the G overnment's decision to discontinue the target -oriented and revenue -centric approach for 
disinvestment. The Committee urged the Ministry to ensure that disinvestment should not become 
any less of a priority and be carried out in the right spirit with the a im of enhancing operational 
efficiency and maximising long -term value for Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) and 
optimising returns for the Government.

(i) Hindustan Aeronautics Limited  
The Alternative Mechanism (AM), on the recommendations of the High -Level Committee (HLC), 
approved (22 March 2023) the disinvestment of 1.7 5 per cent of the paid -up equity of Hindustan 
Aeronautics Limited (HAL) through Offer for Sale (OFS) with an option to sell additional shares up 
to 1.75 per cent of the paid-up equity in case of over-subscription. 
The OFS of HAL was launched on 23 March 2023 and 3.50 per cent of the total paid -up equity of 
HAL was sold resulting in receipts of ₹2,901.09 crore. Further, Employee OFS (0.0113 per cent) of 
HAL was completed in April 2023. GoI’s shareholding in HAL was r educed to 71.64 percent after 
completion of the OFS. 
As per clause no. 4.1 of SEBI regulations (January 2023), an advertisement about the offer for sale 
through Stock Exchanges is to be released after the announcement/ notice of the offer for sale of 
shares has been made available to the Stock Exchanges. DIPAM vide its letters dated 22 March and 
23 March 2023 requested HAL to take necessary action and ensure release of advertisement on 23 
March 2023 and 24 March 2023 at Central Bureau of Communication (erst while DAVP) rates 
through an advertisement agency of the company. The expenditure was to be first borne by the 
Company and later be reimbursed by DIPAM. 

 
 
 
174 
Audit observed that DIPAM had reimbursed an amount of ₹21.11 lakh (over and above the DAVP 
rates) towards advertisement expenditure incurred at non -DAVP rates. The reason quoted by HAL 
for advertising at non-DAVP rates was that some of the newspapers did not extend the DAVP rates 
to them as they considered HAL as a commercial organisation. Audit, however, o bserved that the 
advertisement which appeared in the newspapers was in the name of ‘Ministry of Defence’ and was 
on behalf of the President of India regarding offer for sale of the equity shares of HAL.  
DIPAM replied (September 2025) that since the purchase order for advertisement was placed by HAL 
and the invoice was to be raised in the name of HAL, some of the newspapers did not agree for the 
DAVP rates. Further, all the formalities including obtaining necessary approvals etc. for OFS 
transaction were re quired to be completed in a sequential order, in a very short time span starting 
from late afternoon up to late evening of the previous day of the Transaction day. Since the 
Newspapers are normally approached in the late evening of T -1 day, there was a ver y limited time 
frame available for placing the order by the concerned CPSE. At the time of reimbursement, the 
explanation given by HAL was duly considered by DIPAM and with the concurrence of IFU and 
approval of competent authority, the reimbursement was made by DIPAM. 
The reply may be viewed in light of the fact that since the OFS transactions were being undertaken 
by GoI and the advertisements were made in the name of GoI, non-extension of DAVP rates was not 
justified. DIPAM could have taken up the matter  with the Central Bureau of Communication about 
charging of non DAVP rates by some of the newspapers for advertisement published on behalf of the 
GoI or its Departments, after the transaction was completed, since Newspaper agencies were 
contractually bound to extend DAVP rates for GoI related advertisements. 
(ii) Rail Vikas Nigam Limited  
The Alternative Mechanism, based on the recommendation of the HLC, approved (26 July 2023) 
disinvestment of 3.4 per cent of the paid up equity shares in Rail Vikas Nigam Limited (RVNL) with 
an option to sell additional shares upto 1.96 per cent of the paid up equity in case of over-subscription, 
out of the Government’s current shareholding of 78.20 per cent. The bidding took place on 27 July 
2023 under non -retail category a nd there was oversubscription by 273.46 per cent. In view of the 
over-subscription, DIPAM exercised the option to sell additional shares equal to 1.96 per cent of the 
paid up equity capital. Accordingly, DIPAM realised a total of ₹1365.61 crore through disinvestment 
and the Government’s shareholding was reduced to 72.84 per cent.  
DIPAM had asked (23 March 2021) RVNL to publish advertisements in various newspapers at DAVP 
rates for the purpose of OFS (first tranche), the cost of which was to be reimbursed b y DIPAM. 
Accordingly, RVNL got the advertisements published in various newspapers on 24 March 2021 and 
25 March 2021, through a private agency. After publication, the Agency raised the invoice dated 25 
March 2021 on RVNL for an amount of ₹36.99 lakh includ ing GST of ₹1.76 lakh, which was duly 
paid by RVNL. Subsequently, RVNL asked DIPAM to reimburse the cost of advertisement 
amounting to ₹36.99 lakh which was reimbursed by DIPAM.  
Audit observed that since the GST invoice had been raised on RVNL and the same was duly paid by 
RVNL, the GST input credit was available with RNVL and as such the amount of GST should not 

 
 
 
175 
have been reimbursed to RVNL by DIPAM. This resulted in overpayment of ₹1.76 lakh to RVNL by 
DIPAM.

3.1.2 Buy-back of shares 
As per the guidelines (May 2016) on Capital restructuring of CPSEs, surplus cash and bank balance 
with the CPSE shall be considered for restructuring of capital through buyback. Further, every CPSE 
having net -worth of at least ₹2,000 crore and cash and bank balance of over ₹1,000 crore shall 
exercise the option to buy-back their shares.  These guidelines shall not apply to the companies which 
have been set up under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013 or which have accumulated losses. In 
case any CPSE is not able to comply with these guidelines, specific exempt ion has to be obtained 
from DIPAM through its Administrative Ministry/Department. For this purpose, an Inter-Ministerial 
Committee for Monitoring of Capital Management and Dividend in CPSEs (CMCDC) had been 
constituted (September 2020) by DIPAM to decide on the exemption proposals of CPSEs. 
During the financial year 2023-24, no transaction of buy-back of shares was reported by DIPAM.

holdings of the shares and deposits maintained by it.  
Audit observed that SUUTI remitted (March 2024) dividend income of ₹1,770 crore to DIPAM which 
was reported by DIPAM as part of the Disinvestment receipts for the year 2023-24 (Annual Report). 
Since the income is not a part of remittance from sale of Government Shareholdings, it should not be 
included in disinvestment receipts. Further, this amount was booked un der the head Miscellaneous 
Capital Receipt- Disinvestment of Public Sector and Other Undertakings (Head of Account: 4000 03

Manager.

190 170 100). This had resulted in overstatement of disinvestment receipts by ₹1,770 crore for the

companies were still with CEPI and had not been transferred to the Transaction Advisor due to 
various reasons. 
The Transaction Advisor further informed the reasons for non -disposal of the shares of listed 
companies being that some of these companies are listed on regional exchanges which had been non-
operational in some cases, trading had been suspended on account of non -compliance and some 
company stocks had seen negligible or very low trading volumes and suggested that a different 
methodology needed to be adopted for selling these shares. 
DIPAM sought (March 2023) clarification from SEBI and SEBI replied that the sale of enemy shares 
of listed companies which were either having negligible or low trading volumes or were listed on 
non-operational exchanges may be executed through an off -market transaction.  A note dated 15 
September 2023 was put up for approval of Alternative Mechanism in which HLC proposed the 
detailed methodology to be adopted for sale of remaining enemy shares of unlisted an d listed 
companies. The Alternative Mechanism approved the recommendation of the HLC on 1 October 
2023. An advertisement was issued (11 January 2024) in the newspapers for the sale of 2,91,536 
shares of 84 companies. However, 13,158 shares of two companies  were later on withdrawn and 
hence 2,78,378 shares were left for sale. 
As per the minutes of the HLC meeting held on 14 February 2024, an Inter -Ministerial Committee 
(IMC) was constituted to open and tabulate the financial bids. IMC opened the bids on 9 Fe bruary 
2024 and thereafter handed over the same to Transaction Advisor for further evaluation. The 
Transaction Advisor received an amount of ₹31.70 crore from sale of 1,44,692 shares (out of 2,78,378 
shares) and allotted the shares to the bidders and intimated the same to DIPAM on 9 April 2024.  
In this regard, Audit observed the following: 
(i) The date(s) when the amount was received by the Transaction Advisor (TA) from the bidders 
and the date/(s) when the same amount was transferred to CEPI was not available  in files/ 
records provided to Audit by DIPAM. Further, DIPAM had not shown any amount from sale 
of enemy shares under disinvestment proceeds for FY 2023-24, as per information available on 
the DIPAM website.

CEPI, which was further deposited by CEPI to the Consolidated Fund of India. Taking into an account 
that the amount had already been deposited to CFI, the same was updated in the disinvestment 
proceeds maintained by DIPAM (in 2024-25).

7.7.2 Status of closure of Subsidiaries/ Units by Holding/ Parent PSEs. 
The Cabinet in its meeting held on 18 May 2022 had empowered the Board  of Directors of the 
Holding/Parent Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) to recommend and undertake the process for 
disinvestment (both strategic disinvestment and minority stake sale)/ closure of their subsidiaries/ 
units/ stake in Joint Ventures. Proposal in this regard shall be submitted by the Parent/ Holding PSEs 
to DIPAM through its Administrative Ministry. DIPAM shall take ‘in principle’ approval of the 
proposal from the Alternative Mechanism (AM). DIPAM had notified the above decisions of the 
Cabinet vide OM dated 1 June 2022. 
DIPAM issued (14 September 2022) guiding principles for strategic disinvestment/minority stake 
sale of subsidiaries/units/sale of stakes in Joint Ventures by the holding/parent PSEs, whereas DPE 
issued (31 October 2022) guiding principles for closure of subsidiaries/units by their holding/parent 
PSEs. As per the timelines specified in the guiding principles, the process of closure of the 
subsidiary/units should be completed within 8 months and 15 days from the date of ‘in principle 
approval’ of closure by the AM.  
As per the Annual Report (2023-24) of the Ministry of Finance (Chapter IV), DIPAM in accordance 
with the new policy took approval of AM, for closure/disinvestment of eight subsidiaries/units of 
PSEs (Annexure XLI), out of which two subsidiaries were approved for disinvestment and six were 
approved for closure. Out of the six subsidiaries approved for closure, only two had been closed and 
four had not been closed till date.

CHAPTER VIII

Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) issued National Voluntary Guidelines (NVGs) on Social, 
Environmental and Economic Responsibilities of Business in 2011 towards sustainability reporting. 
Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) in 2012, mandated top 100 listed companies to file 
Business Responsibility Report (BRR) in line with NVGs, which was subsequently extended to top 
500 listed companies in 2016 and to top 1000 listed companies in 2019. 
In 2019, MCA, as a revision from NVGs, formulated the National Guidelines on Responsible 
Business Conduct (NGRBC), having nine principles. These guidelines were intended  to assist 
businesses to embrace the principle of responsible conduct beyond the requirements of regulatory 
compliance. SEBI in May 2021, in line with NGRBC, introduced reporting requirements on 
Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) parameters in the form of Business Responsibility and 
Sustainability Reporting (BRSR) framework by replacing the earlier BRR. BRSR was intended 
towards having quantitative and standardized disclosures to enable comparability across companies, 
sectors and time.  
In July 2023, SEBI modified the BRSR framework to strengthen assurance and enhance disclosure 
requirements for listed entities. As per the regulations, for the financial year 2023 -24, the top 1000 
listed companies in India by market capitalisation as of 31 March 2024 shall make disclosures as per 
the updated BRSR format, as part of their Annual Reports. Further, the Annual Report is to be 
submitted to the stock exchange and also to be published on their website. Additionally, the top 150 
listed entities shall mandatorily undertake reasonable assurance for the BRSR Core disclosures from 
the assurance provider having no conflict of interest with the entity. 
 
i. To assess whether all the applicable BRSR disclosures, as mandated, were complied with by 
listed CPSEs, in a manner verifiable with available documentary evidence, and  
ii. To assess the adequacy of internal controls in listed CPSEs to support BRSR reporting

Audit selected 30 listed CPSEs (Annexure XLII) for review of BRSR disclosure for the financial 
year ending March 2024. Out of the selected CPSEs, 18 CPSEs are within the top 150 listed 
companies, who require reasonable assurance on the BRSR Core disclosure. Remaining 12 listed 
CPSEs are only mandated to report under BRSR Framework. 
Audit examined the completeness and verifiability of BRSR disclosures wherein verifiability of 
disclosures was based on the availability of supporting documents provided by the CPSEs. The review 
of indicators was restricted to examination of the appropriateness of the facts reported for the 
indicators.  
The names of CPSEs have been masked by using masking codes, viz. CPSE_1 to CPSE_30. 
 
Review was carried out based on: 
i. SEBI Circulars related to BRSR format and assurance requirement.  
ii. Guidance Note for BRSR Format issued by SEBI.  
iii. FAQs issued by National Security Exchange (NSE) and Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) 
 
BRSR framework is structured into the following three sections comprising of 145 indicators:  
i. Section A – General Disclosure (26 indicators) – captures basic information about the entity. 
ii. Section B – Management and Process Disclosure (12 indicators). 
iii. Section C – Principle-wise Performance Disclosure. Section C is divided into nine principles 
which seek disclosure on the performance of entity. Reporting under nine principles is divided 
into 68 essential indicators and 39 leadership indicators.  
BRSR reporting was divided into essential and leadership indicators. The essential indicators were 
required to be reported on a mandatory basis, while the reporting of leadership indicators was 
voluntary. 
Audit reviewed the above indicators across selected CPSEs, and section/ principle wise audit findings 
are discussed in subsequent paragraphs. 
8.5.1 Section A: General Disclosure  
Section A contains 26 indicators on general information about the entity including its business 
activities, operational locations, and key details about its subsidiaries and employees.

8.5.3  Section C: Principle wise performance disclosure  
Section C aimed at helping entities to demonstrate their performance in integrating the Principles and 
Core Elements with key processes and decisions. Section C has nine principles, containing a total of 
107 indicators. The information sought is categorize d as "Essential" and "Leadership". While the 
essential indicators are expected to be disclosed by every entity that is mandated to file this report, 
the leadership indicators may be voluntarily disclosed by entities.  
8.5.3.1 Principle 1: Businesses should  conduct and govern themselves with integrity, and in 
manner that is Ethical, Transparent and Accountable  
Principle 1 contains 11 indicators (nine Essential indicators and two Leadership indicators) which

Principle 4 containing five indicators (two essential indicators and three leadership indicators) 
emphasizes that businesses should respect and safeguard the interests of all stakeholders, especially 
the vulnerable and marginalized, by maximizing positive impacts and minimizing adverse effects of

Review revealed that out of 30 CPSEs, no discrepancies were observed in 26 CPSEs. In case of

Principle 4 are presented in Annexure XLVIII. 
Highlights of the deficiencies noticed in Principle 4 were as under: 
 Vulnerable and Marginalized Group : Entity was required to disclose the list of key

vulnerable and marginalized group. SEBI has identified group of individuals who are unable to 
realize their rights  or enjoy opportunities due to adverse physical, mental, social, economic, 
cultural, political, geographic or health circumstances such as women, persons with disabilities 
(PWD), Scheduled Castes/ Scheduled Tribes (SC/ST), displaced/ landless small/ margin al 
farmers, migrant workers, etc. as vulnerable and marginalized group.  
 Review revealed that in four CPSEs (viz. CPSE_4, CPSE_13, CPSE_14 and CPSE_20) 
disclosures made were not in line with the requirements of BRSR framework.  
 CPSE_4 involves mining activities by acquiring land and subsequent, rehabilitation and 
resettlement. However, while making the disclosure, CPSE_4 did not consider/disclose 
the displaced/landless farmers as vulnerable and marginalized groups under the 
stakeholder group “Land Loser”, against the mandate. 
 Two CPSEs (CPSE_4, and CPSE_20) did not consider PWD employees under 
marginalized/vulnerable group, contrary to the format and their respective Annual 
Reports. 
 Despite making procurement from the enterprises/MSMEs owned by SC/ST and women 
entrepreneurs, three CPSEs (CPSE_4, CPSE_13 and CPSE_14), have not considered 
them as marginalized and vulnerable in “Suppliers and Contractors” category.

8.5.4  Deficiencies in Internal Control 
Internal Control System means the procedures adopted by the entity to ensure the accuracy and 
completeness of the records, preparation of reliable information and reporting thereof. 
Review revealed the systemic deficiencies in the internal control environment governing BRSR 
reporting among CPSEs under review, in the areas of documentation, data accuracy, assurance 
mechanisms which are as under: 
8.5.4.1  Non-Compliance with Assurance Requirements  
SEBI mandate (Ju ly 2023) that top 150 listed entities are required to obtaining the reasonable 
assurance on BRSR Core from the third -party assurance provider. SEBI prescribed a format for 
furnishing the assurance by third-party assurance provider.  
Audit observed that: 
 Out of 30 CPSEs, 18 CPSEs were required to obtain reasonable assurance. Audit observed no 
discrepancies in 16 CPSEs.  
 In case of one CPSE (CPSE_28) third party assurance provider was engaged to perform limited 
assurance, resulting in non-compliance of SEBI requirement.  
 In CPSE_4, assurance provider issued the assurance statement on BRSR format instead of 
BRSR core.  
These lapses indicate that the assurance process failed to meet the intended objective of enhancing 
the reliability and integrity of disclosures and also did not align with the laid down requirements. 
CPSE_4 noted the audit observation while the response from CPSE_28 was not received till 
finalisation of the report (21 August 2025). 
MoC and MoR accepted (January 2026) the audit observation and assured to make necessary changes 
in subsequent reports. 
8.5.4.2  Non-adherence to BRSR framework in the new updated format 
SEBI, in May 2021, introduced reporting requirements on Environmental, Social and Governance 
parameters in BRSR framework. This reporting framework was revised in July 2023 with the 
introduction of BRSR Core framework, aiming to strengthen assurance m echanism and enhance 
disclosure requirements for listed entities. 
Audit observed that one CPSE (CPSE_16) has not submitted its BRSR report as per the revised format 
prescribed by SEBI in July 2023. All the remaining CPSEs have made the disclosure in the requisite 
format. 

 
 
 
216 
While accepting the audit observation, the CPSE has assured that appropriate disclosure would be 
made in future reports.  
8.5.4.3  Other issues 
 Incorrect and partial Disclosures: Audit came across instances wherein the disclosure, by the 
CPSEs in the BRSR report, were inconsistent/ not matching with the information given in the 
annual report or the documents so made available by the entity. Also, there are instances of 
partial disclosure/ non -compliances of disclosure requirements, which h ave been highlighted 
with the respective indicators.  
The above deficiencies indicate absence of standard operating procedures for data collection, 
validation, and documentation which resulted in inaccuracy in reporting. 
8.5.5  Data Collection Mechanism and Challenges in preparation of BRSR 
Data collection mechanism and challenges in preparation of BRSR were examined in sampled CPSEs 
as detailed below: 
 Data Collection and Reporting Mechanism 
In 19 CPSEs, BRSR reports were compiled and prepared through dep artmental resources, whereas 
11 CPSEs120 engaged external agencies for the compilation and preparation of the reports. In these 
11 CPSEs, preparation of the report was based on the data furnished by the respective entities. 
 Absence of Dedicated Systems/ modules and Policies 
Audit examined whether there is dedicated system/ module in prevailing IT environment. CPSEs had 
not developed any dedicated data collection modules or tools specifically for BRSR reporting. 
Furthermore, no internal policies or guidelines were formulated to govern the preparation and 
compilation of BRSR reports. 
 Capacity Building Efforts 
Two CPSE (CPSE_1 and CPSE_10) have taken initiatives towards capacity building to strengthen 
BRSR reporting by arranging workshops and training sessions. 
 Challenges in Data Consolidation 
The consolidation of data from diverse business units into a standardized BRSR format, unavailability 
of centralised data management platform, compilation and quantification of environment data were 
identified as major challenges faced by CPSEs, impacting the efficiency and quality of reporting. 
MoC, Ministry of Defense for CPSE_2 and CPSE_3, MoR for CPSE_6 and CPSE_13, MoHUA, 
MoP for CPSE_20 and Ministry of Shipping responded (January 2026) that efforts are being made  
                                                           
120CPSE_4, CPSE_8, CPSE_9, CPSE_13, CPSE_17, CPSE_19, CPSE_21, CPSE_22, CPSE_23, CPSE_24 and 
CPSE_28 

 
 
 
217 
for refining the reporting process for BRSR, as per SEBI mandated framework for ESG disclosures, 
in future. 
 
BRSR framework was issued by SEBI to enhance the disclosure requirements and to strengthen the 
assurance by the entities in respect of Environmental, Social and Governance parameters. Audit 
noticed instances of non-compliances and inconsistencies in the BRSR reports of the selected CPSEs 
in respect of disclosure requirements as mandated by SEBI. While making the disclosures in the 
BRSR report, Audit noticed incorrect disclosures and partial disclosures against the stipulations 
which have been highlighted in the Report. There were instances wherein the disclosures so made in 
the BRSR report by the CPSEs were inconsistent with the information disclosed in their own Annual 
Reports.

29 Northern 
Coalfields 
Limited
GC •	 Coal India Limited, while issuing (September 2020) accounting 
instruction on Over Burden Removal (OBR), instructed that 
cost not directly associated with the OBR activity would be 
excluded from determining the OB cost for valuation of advance 
stripping and ratio variance reserve. Contrary to the above, 
Nigahi and Jayant Projects of NCL included administrative and 
audit expenses, medical reimbursements, postage, printing and 
stationery etc. in arriving at Stripping Activity Adjustment after 
ratio variance adjustments, to be charged to the Statement of 
Profit & Loss of these units. Since the stated costs were not 
directly related to OBR, these should not have been apportioned 
under OBR activity, which otherwise resulted in understatement 
of Stripping Activity Adjustment with corresponding 
overstatement of Profit. Nature and items of cost not directly 
related with OBR activity needs to be judiciously identified and 
demarcated from other costs in arriving at precise allocation of 
costs between coal and OBR, and uniformity in such accounting 
treatment across all areas / mines needs to be ensured. 
A uniform format was circulated and 
implemented across all units to maintain 
consistency in cost allocation between coal 
and overburden. This came into effect from 
the June 2023.

in FY 2022-23 and equity has reduced in both the entities and
